That being said, part of what we do when we’re talking to customers about, hey, an agent is now going to do this work is actually around reallocation. I don’t think any business would claim like once we have this solved, there’s nothing for this group of people to work on and try to solve. So our approach really is about what can we replace and then what are the next biggest problems to look at?

36:05 and I’d make an argument in most large companies that that cycle kind of continues forever. There’s always the next problem if I think about how we’ve grown. Infinite demands. There’s always been another problem and actually taking those people that may have this like super deep subject matter expert and bringing them above water to start to maybe work more across teams or like think about parts of the business less so on like the level of a sell in a spreadsheet and more about how these teams are working together. Ultimately, in the long run, I think that keeps most people there

36:41 and allows those businesses to become more nimble and actually tackle the big meaty problems and not the drudge of most people’s day-to-day. When you’re thinking about someone that’s in a finance division, they’re mostly in spreadsheets, but how can we elevate them to think strategically about the business and where money is allocated and things like that. Yeah, and I also feel like when we have these conversations around job displacement or job reallocation, we talk about it as this thing happening to people. And one of the reasons I don’t like that is I feel like it doesn’t give enough credit to people

37:17 to have agency in their own lives, meaning I think... You can adjust. Yeah, people really should be thinking. When I think about enablement or people re-skilling, I think it is the job of an employer because they want to drive growth in their business, but it is also the job of an employee. And I think when people say that AI is going to replace all of the work that people don’t enjoy doing, I think that’s a little bit of like cope for the reality of just people are going to be put out of jobs because a lot of people don’t have the luxury of liking or not liking a job. They do a job to make money. And also I think people, to the extent that it’s possible,

37:53 should have agency in saying to themselves, okay what is the the stability or replaceability of my job over the next few years and if i am to try to skill up in a way that i’m better protected what does that look like people have agency to say that to themselves and actually take action yeah yeah yeah um i think that’s a good message for people to reflect on um the last piece i wanted to touch on before i let you guys go is just new york um you know uh greatest city in the world according to some people some people what’s the mood generally among the people they talk to, whether it’s at work, personally, what’s the feeling, right?

38:28 I live in San Francisco all day long. Everyone’s just in agents all day long. The discussion is instincts or grok or muse. It’s not like do you like AI or not, right? And I feel like I want to step out of that bubble for a bit, but it’s still New York. It’s still progressive. It’s still forward-looking. Yeah. I mean, what I’d say is I feel like, basically, I would just say there’s a bubble in New York that is a smaller bubble than exists in SF. If SF is like a big bubble, I think we at Tenex feel like, you know, we are in a, what I would say is like a microcosm of San Francisco

39:03 because of the people that self-select to work at the company. And then also the companies that we’re partnered with and like the people that we engage with in New York. But I would for sure say also, it is true that it is a smaller universe than like in SF, when you go to SF, it feels all encompassing where it’s like everyone, everywhere you look, There was someone who, similar to AIE, how I was saying earlier when I went on stage, if people go on Twitter or X because they feel like they’re on Edge City, they’re living in the future, AIE is that on steroids. I feel like SF is similar to AIE.

39:40 I mean, it’s probably the overlap of AIE generally and people who have lived at some point in their life in SF is probably a very large overlap. We’re roughly 1% of the city now. Actually? For World’s Fair, yeah. That’s crazy. Yeah. But like to that point, I just think like it is in the culture and the DNA of SF where a very big population of people live in the future. I think you can find that group in New York. And I think we at Tenex have found that people. And part of our goal is to drive like AI as a hub or New York as a hub for

40:16 AI in the US because there is so much commerce here that like it is going to be a place where diffusion of the technology actually has such a meaningful impact on the GDP of this country. I think the bubble is smaller now and we take it almost as like a charge of ours to increase our bubble. Maybe I don’t know that it’s possible to get to SF size, but I do think we can have a meaningful impact on getting more people to live in the future here. There’s a physical, like you see it on the billboards. It’s slowly creeping in. Oh, totally. People used to, remember the friend campaign where people would like spray all sorts of graffiti on that? I think that was like a little bit of an intentional rage bait. But now you have the unironic AI billboards and people are like, I guess

40:52 that’s part of life now. A hundred percent. Yeah, so I think it’s like, I think there’s an opportunity to bring kind of like the edge and like the, just like the living in the future nature that SF has created because of just like the economic climate that exists there because of venture, because of tech companies, then because of the people that are attracted there. but I also think of us as like we’re in a, it’s weird, we’re in a smaller pond for AI but I would argue we’re in as big of a pond if not a bigger pond for like

41:29 commercial value and so I actually the way I put it is like the reason I do AI in New York is I bring all the people from San Francisco to come here and meet their customers and also get a reality check Totally. And I actually think there’s a really interesting arbitrage there. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, totally. Okay, awesome. Call for hiring. I know you guys are always hiring. Yep. What are you hiring for? What’s changed? Yep. We’re hiring forward deployed engineers at Tenex. Just go to tenex.co. We’re also always hiring AI strategists, which are basically technical consultants who are leading client engagements. And the team is 75 strong in New York City. We’re continuing to make New

42:07 York City our home. And then if you are an enterprise who is looking to actually get AI native and you’ve tried it, it’s not working, hit us up. I promise we’ll do better work than, not going to name them, but a lot of other traditional consultancies. Ooh, spicy. CJ? Yeah, I mean, I echo all of that. I’m particularly looking for engineers. What’s a special project? What is that? A special project involves anything outside of kind of our client work. So I think about my brain right now. It is building that meta harness and system internally that basically it’s

42:45 like find the bleeding edge of what the models can do and give them tools to augment how well they can do it. And then also internally working on the platform that Alex mentioned. big goal there, diffuse these background agents and actually get them out to enterprises in a way that’s truly, truly helpful to them. Yeah. And solve a lot of those like messy IT problems that we hit on earlier. Dude, when you have some solutions, we take guest posts on the Latent Space blog. I’d love to welcome some sharing of knowledge. But otherwise, thank you so much for your time.

43:20 And good to see you again in New York. Yeah, likewise. Appreciate it. Once a year, once a year. Hell yeah. Thank you.

items.title: Les di una oficina a mis agentes de IA, y ahora mi equipo puede verlos trabajar
items.summary: Este artículo es la versión en español de I gave my AI coding agents an office, and now my team can watch them work . Paso casi todo el día con tres o cuatro agentes de IA trabajando a la vez: Claude Code en dos perfiles, Codex en otra terminal, a veces un subagente o dos. Son buena compañía, pero invisible. La única forma de saber que uno lleva cinco minutos esperando mi permiso es revisar terminal por terminal. Así que les hice una oficina. deskmates es una oficina pixel-art donde cada sesión de un agente en tu equipo es un personaje en su escritorio. Entra cuando la sesión empieza, escribe mientras edita, lee mientras busca, levanta un signo de pregunta amarillo cuando necesita tu permiso y se va cuando la sesión termina. Los subagentes se sientan al lado del agente que los lanzó y, cuando terminan, pasan por su escritorio con un documento antes de irse. Es código abierto (MIT) y se instala con un comando: npm install -g deskmates deskmates serve # http://127.0.0.1:47821 deskmates demo # agentes simulados, por si quieres verlo antes de conectar nada Cómo entran los agentes Cada herramienta le cuenta a deskmates lo que hace a su manera, y todo termina convertido en el mismo evento pequeño: Claude Code , mediante hooks. deskmates connect los agrega a la configuración de un perfil, marcados para que disconnect quite solo los suyos. El hook son unas pocas líneas de shell con un tope de 50 ms que siempre termina con código 0: nunca debe frenar a un agente. Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor y Gemini CLI , mediante los archivos de sesión que ya escriben. Sin configuración. Cualquier otra cosa , mediante una pequeña API HTTP de ingesta o un servidor MCP, para que un script, un job de CI u otro agente también pueda entrar. Desde ahí los datos van en un solo sentido: eventos, deduplicación, un reducer puro que decide quién está trabajando, esperando, libre, dormido o saliendo, y un WebSocket que alimenta la página. La página es un canvas con una simulación de actores encima: caminan por una cuadrícula de casillas, toman descansos en las máquinas expendedoras, se reúnen cuando dos agentes del mismo proyecto están libres, y hay mascotas que pasean entre las salas. La privacidad fue la primera regla, no la última Una oficina que muestra lo que hacen tus agentes podría mostrar demasiado con mucha facilidad. Los eventos llevan solo el nombre de una herramienta y un detalle de 120 caracteres como máximo: un nombre de archivo o la primera línea de un comando. Los prompts, el contenido de los archivos y la salida de las herramientas nunca salen de los adaptadores, y el historial diario guarda conteos, no contenido. Nada sale de tu equipo a menos que lo pidas. Después terminó en el TV de la oficina Al lado de mi teclado no era donde la quería. La quería en una tablet, y después en la pantalla de la oficina. deskmates serve --lan la sirve en tu red detrás de un token, imprime un QR en la terminal, y la página tiene un botón para compartir con el mismo QR y un modo kiosco que llena la pantalla. En un TV eso significó aprender sobre píxeles de dispositivo: la oficina se dibuja a escalas enteras para que el pixel art se vea nítido, y el modo kiosco la estira para llenar la pantalla cuando eso importa más. La oficina compartida Ver solo a mis agentes me aburrió rápido. Varios de nosotros usamos agentes de programación, así que la última pieza fue una oficina compartida: # en un equipo al que todos puedan llegar deskmates serve --lan --shared # en cada PC deskmates serve --relay http://lab:47821 --name "Jesús" Cada PC envía los mismos eventos pequeños a la oficina compartida, donde llegan al piso Headquarters: seis islas de cuatro escritorios, cada una con el color de su PC, una sala de estar, una mesa de reuniones y un café en el medio. Cuando agentes de PCs distintas esperan permiso al mismo tiempo, se van al café a conversar. Es la función más inútil que escribí este año, y mi favorita. Lo que aprendí Núcleo puro, bordes visuales. El reducer y la escena son funciones deterministas de los eventos y del tiempo. Eso hizo que casi todo se pudiera probar sin navegador, y las pruebas en el navegador comparan capturas píxel por píxel. El piso tuvo que convertirse en datos. La oficina compartida empezó con la misma sala pequeña repetida una al lado de otra. Un solo piso grande obligó a convertir las constantes de la sala en un valor que los temas pueden declarar. Todas las capturas existentes tenían que quedar idénticas mientras eso pasaba, y esa regla atrapó más errores que cualquier revisión. Los agentes revisan código mejor de lo que esperaba, y leen capturas peor que yo. Construí casi todo esto con Claude Code, con un agente nuevo revisando cada cambio. Encontraron errores reales de concurrencia y de casos límite; las imágenes las tuve que mirar yo, una por una. Pruébalo Repositorio: https://github.com/Jfernandez27/deskmates?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=deskmates Instalación: npm install -g deskmates , después deskmates serve y deskmates connect Node 22.18 o superior Si trabajas con varios agentes al día, me gustaría saber qué señal extrañas más cuando trabajan en segundo plano. Eso es lo que decide qué aprende la oficina después.

  • Cualquier otra cosa, mediante una pequeña API HTTP de ingesta o un servidor MCP, para que un script, un job de CI u otro agente también pueda entrar.

Desde ahí los datos van en un solo sentido: eventos, deduplicación, un reducer puro que decide quién está trabajando, esperando, libre, dormido o saliendo, y un WebSocket que alimenta la página. La página es un canvas con una simulación de actores encima: caminan por una cuadrícula de casillas, toman descansos en las máquinas expendedoras, se reúnen cuando dos agentes del mismo proyecto están libres, y hay mascotas que pasean entre las salas.

La privacidad fue la primera regla, no la última

Una oficina que muestra lo que hacen tus agentes podría mostrar demasiado con mucha facilidad. Los eventos llevan solo el nombre de una herramienta y un detalle de 120 caracteres como máximo: un nombre de archivo o la primera línea de un comando. Los prompts, el contenido de los archivos y la salida de las herramientas nunca salen de los adaptadores, y el historial diario guarda conteos, no contenido. Nada sale de tu equipo a menos que lo pidas.

Después terminó en el TV de la oficina

Al lado de mi teclado no era donde la quería. La quería en una tablet, y después en la pantalla de la oficina.

deskmates serve --lan la sirve en tu red detrás de un token, imprime un QR en la terminal, y la página tiene un botón para compartir con el mismo QR y un modo kiosco que llena la pantalla. En un TV eso significó aprender sobre píxeles de dispositivo: la oficina se dibuja a escalas enteras para que el pixel art se vea nítido, y el modo kiosco la estira para llenar la pantalla cuando eso importa más.

La oficina compartida

Ver solo a mis agentes me aburrió rápido. Varios de nosotros usamos agentes de programación, así que la última pieza fue una oficina compartida:

# en un equipo al que todos puedan llegar
deskmates serve --lan --shared

# en cada PC
deskmates serve --relay http://lab:47821 --name "Jesús"

Cada PC envía los mismos eventos pequeños a la oficina compartida, donde llegan al piso Headquarters: seis islas de cuatro escritorios, cada una con el color de su PC, una sala de estar, una mesa de reuniones y un café en el medio. Cuando agentes de PCs distintas esperan permiso al mismo tiempo, se van al café a conversar. Es la función más inútil que escribí este año, y mi favorita.

Lo que aprendí
  • Núcleo puro, bordes visuales. El reducer y la escena son funciones deterministas de los eventos y del tiempo. Eso hizo que casi todo se pudiera probar sin navegador, y las pruebas en el navegador comparan capturas píxel por píxel.
  • El piso tuvo que convertirse en datos. La oficina compartida empezó con la misma sala pequeña repetida una al lado de otra. Un solo piso grande obligó a convertir las constantes de la sala en un valor que los temas pueden declarar. Todas las capturas existentes tenían que quedar idénticas mientras eso pasaba, y esa regla atrapó más errores que cualquier revisión.
  • Los agentes revisan código mejor de lo que esperaba, y leen capturas peor que yo. Construí casi todo esto con Claude Code, con un agente nuevo revisando cada cambio. Encontraron errores reales de concurrencia y de casos límite; las imágenes las tuve que mirar yo, una por una.
Pruébalo
  • Repositorio: https://github.com/Jfernandez27/deskmates?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=deskmates
  • Instalación: npm install -g deskmates, después deskmates serve y deskmates connect
  • Node 22.18 o superior

Si trabajas con varios agentes al día, me gustaría saber qué señal extrañas más cuando trabajan en segundo plano. Eso es lo que decide qué aprende la oficina después.

items.title: Salesforce to Acquire Braze for $5.66 Bn to Strengthen AI Customer Marketing
items.summary: Salesforce has agreed to acquire customer engagement platform Braze for approximately $5.66 billion, as the company looks to expand its marketing capabilities with real-time customer data and AI-powered personalisation. Under the terms of the agreement, Braze Class A shareholders will receive $47.50 per share in cash. The transaction is expected to close in Salesforce’s FY28. The acquisition will bring Braze’s customer engagement platform into Salesforce’s Marketing Cloud, combining its capabilities in real-time messaging and customer journey management with Salesforce’s CRM, Data 360, and Agentforce platforms. “Most of that wow comes from knowing your customer, and responding at just the right moment. Braze was built to turn live customer behaviour into personalised engagement at scale,” Patrick Stokes, President of Applications and Marketing at Salesforce, said in a statement. Salesforce said Braze’s technology is expected to complement four layers of its architecture: Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, and SIForce. Braze enables marketers to coordinate customer interactions across mobile applications, websites, email, SMS, and WhatsApp. Its platform uses event-streaming architecture to process customer activity and update profiles in real time, allowing businesses to adapt messaging and customer journeys based on user behaviour. The company’s BrazeAI platform uses AI to help marketers select content, offers, communication channels, and the timing of customer interactions. Salesforce plans to combine these capabilities with customer data and Agentforce to connect marketing activities with sales, commerce, and customer service. The deal comes as Salesforce expands its use of AI agents across its enterprise software portfolio. “Braze was built on the conviction that marketers and their creativity are a brand’s ultimate competitive advantage,” said Bill Magnuson, CEO and Co-founder of Braze. Braze serves approximately 2,770 customers, including Canva, Dairy Queen, Equinox, Instacart, Urban Outfitters, and Venmo. The company was co-founded by Magnuson and Jon Hyman. Salesforce said the acquisition would support its efforts to expand Customer 360 by combining customer data with real-time engagement across multiple channels.

items.title: ElevenLabs Launches Real-Time Voice AI Models With Up to 98.8% Speech Reasoning Accuracy
items.summary: ElevenLabs has launched Eleven Realtime, a family of speech-to-speech models for building voice agents, with two variants for different workloads, as the company looks to simplify the development of conversational AI systems. Eleven Realtime v1 Mini targets applications such as AI assistants, teachers, and interactive characters, while Eleven Realtime v1 Max targets customer support, lead qualification, and workflows involving multiple steps. The two models give developers a choice between cost and capability requirements. Mini is positioned for applications where conversational interaction is the primary requirement, while Max targets tasks that demand stronger reasoning and tool use. Both models support more than 90 languages and can use any of the more than 17,000 voices in the ElevenLabs library. The models combine speech recognition, turn-taking, voice activity detection, and speech generation into a single system. “You shouldn’t have to become a configuration expert to build a voice agent that sounds natural,” the company said in its announcement. ElevenLabs said the models address challenges such as determining when to respond after a pause, handling interruptions and coordinating voice output with the underlying model. In independent evaluations by Artificial Analysis across three public benchmarks, Eleven Realtime v1 Max outperformed Mini on speech reasoning and tool-use tasks. On Big Bench Audio, which evaluates reasoning through spoken questions and answers, Max answered 98.8% of questions correctly, compared with 75.9% for Mini. Max also recorded an average time to first audio of 0.57 seconds, while Mini took 0.62 seconds, suggesting higher accuracy. However, Mini scored higher on Full-Duplex-Bench, which evaluates conversational dynamics, including pauses, interruptions, turn-taking and backchannels. It scored 95.8%, compared with 94.1% for Max. In the Speech Agent Arena, which compares models through blind live conversations based on human preferences and task success, Max scored 998, while Mini scored 988. The gap was wider on tool-use tasks. Max completed 87.1% of these tasks, compared with 60.3% for Mini. ElevenLabs recommends Max for applications that rely heavily on tool calling and multi-step workflows. Compatible with OpenAI’s Realtime API ElevenLabs is also targeting developers already building voice agents using OpenAI's Realtime API. Eleven Realtime follows OpenAI’s Realtime specifications, allowing developers to switch to ElevenLabs by changing the API endpoint and model name in their existing integrations. The API connects through WebSockets and supports OpenAI’s SDK. However, developers using WebRTC integrations will need to move to WebSockets to use the service. Developers can also access the models through ElevenAgents, the company’s agent platform, which provides deployment across phone, web, WhatsApp, and contact centre channels. The platform includes workflows, knowledge bases, guardrails, testing, and monitoring tools.

items.title: Browsers Block eMudhra Certificates After Key Flaw
items.summary: Bengaluru-based digital trust company eMudhra generated eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) private keys with minimal randomness, which attackers could recover almost instantly. Six of the affected certificates were authorised to issue TLS certificates for websites, potentially allowing attackers to impersonate domains they did not control on systems that still trusted the compromised keys. The other two were intended for code signing. The incident came to light when a security researcher, Wayne, whose identity remains anonymous, demonstrated control of the eight private keys by using them to sign a message. Google’s Chrome Root Program received the report and blocked the public-key hashes of the six TLS-issuing intermediates. Mozilla received its report and had protections available to Firefox users with standard configurations. Its investigation found that all eight affected keys used P-384 elliptic-curve cryptography but had private-key values below 256. P-384 keys should be selected unpredictably from a vast range of possible values. In this case, an attacker could recover each private key by testing at most 255 possible values. The vulnerability lay in the key-generation process, not in a failure of the underlying cryptographic algorithm. Intermediate CAs sit between root certificates and the certificates websites present. Browsers trust these intermediaries to issue certificates that establish a website’s identity. Anyone with a compromised TLS-issuing key could create a fraudulent certificate for a domain they don't control. If the attacker could also intercept or redirect a victim’s connection, they could use the certificate to impersonate the legitimate website or intercept and modify traffic. Google and Mozilla have blocked the affected certificates in their respective trust systems, but protection across the wider internet also depends on other software and trust stores receiving equivalent updates. eMudhra said it generated the certificates during a key-generation ceremony on April 30, 2025. The company said it had deployed only one of the eight affected intermediates in production, and none had issued end-entity certificates. It said internal analysis and publicly available Certificate Transparency records supported this finding. eMudhra added that the incident did not affect its root CA private keys or other intermediate CAs. Its investigation into the incident and its security controls is ongoing. “This incident has no impact on customers using our enterprise applications, digital signature services, or other electronic signature solutions,” said the company in a post on X. Founded in 2008, eMudhra provides public-key infrastructure (PKI), digital signatures, certificate management, authentication and identity and access management products. Its emSign business issues digital certificates, while its emSigner platform supports enterprise digital-signature and document-workflow processes. The company lists organisations including Infosys, Airtel, Kotak Bank, Tata Steel, Amazon, ICICI Bank and Cisco among its emSigner case studies. These enterprise-software relationships are separate from the affected emSign certificate infrastructure. eMudhra shares fell 18% in early trading sessions on NSE on October 21.

items.title: H2DF: Calibrated Target Bands for Controllable Language-Model Unlearning
items.summary: Gradient ascent (GA) is a simple language-model unlearning baseline, but it continues increasing forget loss after useful forgetting has occurred. This unbounded pressure can damage retained utility and make forgotten examples abnormally high-loss. We introduce H2DF, a calibrated target-band objective that applies GA-like pressure below a data-dependent lower target and suppresses, or reverses, that pressure after the target region is reached. The targets are estimated from matched non-member examples before training, so the base objective requires one forget-batch forward/backward pass per optimization step; our reported TOFU variant adds sparse retain replay every tenth step. We instantiate a one-sided objective for TOFU question answering and a two-sided objective for MUSE-News language modeling. Across three TOFU seeds, H2DF obtains a forget NLL of 1.528 with margin 0.049 and retain NLL of 1.165 with margin 0.047, matching GradDiff while using retain replay only every tenth step and showing substantially lower variability than GA. On MUSE-News, H2DF improves retention over GA and NPO and is competitive with SimNPO, but does not dominate it. Ablations show that the upper target reduces overshoot and that validation-based checkpoint selection is important. These results support calibrated target bands as a practical mechanism for controlling forgetting strength, while also exposing sensitivity to random seed and calibration quality.

items.title: AutoTerm-SST: Adaptive Terminology Memory with Zero Session-Time Setup for Streaming Speech Translation
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented speech translation improves rare terminology, but systems such as RASST still assume that users provide a glossary before each session. That assumption is inconvenient for live talks, while merging every domain into one growing glossary eventually places too many irrelevant terms in the same retrieval and prompt competition. We present AutoTerm-SST, an interactive system that removes session-time glossary upload and domain selection. It organizes a large offline terminology catalog into topic slices, matches recent streaming translation context to bilingual slice prototypes, and activates a compact multi-slice working set under fixed retrieval and prompt budgets. On five ACL and five ESO oncology talks, AutoTerm matches a known-domain reference in terminology accuracy (88.3% vs. 88.1%) and mWER-resegmented BLEU (45.09 vs. 45.19), while requiring no domain input. Compared with a one-million-entry merged glossary, it improves terminology accuracy by 3.9 points and BLEU by 2.30. Routing plus four-slice retrieval remains lightweight: the complete system runs at 0.406 RTF, and the vLLM host sustains 32 real-time sessions. The live demo exposes active slices and retrieved terminology as the topic changes, providing zero-setup terminology-aware streaming translation.

items.title: WaveCommitments: Private and Verifiable Speech-Agent Marketplaces
items.summary: Modern speech systems are evolving into ecosystems of autonomous speech agents that speak together, negotiate, and trade assets such as embeddings, spectrograms, or raw data. In such markets, sellers cannot reveal assets for evaluation due to privacy constraints, and buyers cannot price what they cannot test. Thus, we open-source WaveCommitments, an end-to-end design that pairs confidential asset valuation via Data Shapley inside a trusted execution environment with multivariate polynomial commitments. It enables selective openings and tamper-evident provenance to prove that a delivered asset matches the valuation while hiding everything else. Our extensive experiments across three known datasets and various tasks with state-of-the-art encoders, including Whisper, reveal that we speed up the best benchmarks by up to 20x while reducing their proof sizes by up to 39x. We also systematically study how a speaker's value shifts across tasks and encoders, revealing agent-level market prices.

items.title: Multimodal Ambivalence and Hesitancy Recognition with Bidirectional Audio--Text Cross-Attention
items.summary: Ambivalence and hesitancy (A/H) are subtle behavioural states that can be expressed through both what a person says and how it is spoken. This paper presents an audio--text framework for video-level A/H recognition. Full-video transcripts and speech waveforms are encoded using pre-trained multilingual BERT and wav2vec~2.0, respectively, and projected into a shared representation space. Two stacked bidirectional cross-attention blocks allow linguistic tokens to attend to acoustic frames and acoustic frames to attend to linguistic context without requiring explicit temporal alignment. The resulting sequences are aggregated through masked mean pooling and combined using concatenation, element-wise products, and absolute differences for binary classification. We evaluate the model on the subject-independent split of the Behavioural Ambivalence/Hesitancy (BAH) dataset. The proposed system achieves 72.19\% accuracy, 75.00\% precision, 81.13\% recall, 77.95\% A/H F1-score, and 70.16\% Macro-F1 on the test set. These results demonstrate the potential of jointly modelling linguistic and acoustic information for automatic A/H recognition.code at:https://github.com/DorriG/ECCV.

items.title: Mixture of Phonetic Experts Based Low-Rank Adaptation of Conformer Models for Accented English Speech Recognition
items.summary: We present Mixture of Phonetic Experts based Low-Rank Adaptation (MoPE-LoRA), a parameter-efficient adaptation framework for accented English speech recognition. Recent mixture-of-experts approaches typically allocate experts per accent, implicitly treating accent identity as the primary axis of variation. In contrast, we organize adaptation along phonetic categories, motivated by the observation that accent differences are often expressed as systematic distortions of phoneme realization. MoPE-LoRA introduces a fixed set of six low-rank experts aligned with manner-of-articulation classes and performs frame-level routing through a hybrid mechanism that combines phoneme supervision with learned acoustic gating. Because the expert set is shared across accents, the model does not require accent-specific modules and naturally extends to previously unseen accents. Experiments on L2-ARCTIC show that MoPE-LoRA consistently improves over single LoRA and full fine-tuning. items.title: AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) possess broad factual knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but solving complex tasks also requires procedural knowledge about how to act. Existing approaches often represent procedural knowledge through trajectories or bundled skills, limiting flexible reuse across interaction histories. This paper introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently applicable units that represent Intent, When, Do, and Avoid guidance. Building on this representation, we propose AtomSD, an Atom-guided Self-Distillation framework in which the learner continually extracts Procedural Atoms from its own successful trajectories and distills them into the evolving policy through Atom-conditioned supervision and task-reward optimization. Comprehensive experiments show that AtomSD consistently outperforms strong reward-based and distillation methods, exceeding the state-of-the-art baseline by up to 9.31 points in average performance. Further analyses demonstrate that the proposed Procedural Atoms provide effective guidance, highlighting the value of atom-level procedural knowledge for policy learning.

items.title: Do We Need the Largest LLMs for Every Clinical Decision?
items.summary: Large clinical language models often require multi-GPU infrastructure, limiting local deployment. We introduce CERTA, a decision-level statistical certificate that determines when a quantized model may substitute for its native BF16 reference and escalates decisions that cannot be certified to it. Across eleven instruction-tuned models, both general-purpose and domain-adapted, from three families (7-72B), we evaluated 2,500 clinical-verification decisions from de-identified patient contexts (2,484 patients), with patient-disjoint calibration and testing. In the higher-power operational analysis, round-to-nearest 8-bit quantization at BF16 storage served 99.8-100% of held-out decisions across all eleven models; formal finite-sample guarantees were assessed separately using the exact split-sample procedure. In the same operational analysis, the class-conditional 4-bit frontier reduced the amortized, BF16-equivalent deployment cost to 25.8% and 27.3% of the BF16 reference for Qwen2.5-72B and HuatuoGPT-o1-72B, respectively, with measured peak memory of 43.0 and 42.7 GB, below the nominal capacity of a single 48 GB accelerator. Deployment on that specific hardware was not directly tested. Under the exact split-sample certificate, which also accounts for configuration selection, these costs were 26.7% and 27.9%. On external disease named-entity benchmarks against human annotations, the frontier-selected NF4 configurations had a mean absolute F1 change of 0.045 on both datasets, with substantial model-specific variation. CERTA converts compression from a fixed precision choice into a risk-controlled deployment policy for this verification task.

items.title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks- MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP, a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues, and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K-1M characters. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG.

items.title: A Multi-granularity Interaction Network for Relational Triple Extraction
items.summary: Relational triple extraction identifies entity relations from raw sentences without depending on entity type information. The performance of traditional methods is seriously degenerated by ``unseen'' entities, because these methods can't build contextual dependencies relevant ``unseen'' entities. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a multi-granularity interaction network that leverages word-word, entity-relation, and head-tail interactions to capture deep semantic dependencies. By incorporating multiple iterations, the multi-granularity interaction network is effective to refine the representations corresponding to head and tail entities. It enhances the global semantic features associated with relational triples, aiding in the remediation of triples that may have been overlooked or omitted in earlier steps. Strong and consistent performance is achieved by our method on two rearranged datasets, with a significant improvement in identifying relational triples, including those involving ``unseen'' named entities. For example, our model improves F1-score by 3.1%/20.5% over previous approaches on the NYT-R/WebNLG-R datasets in the Unseen metric. Code: https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/Interaction-Network.

items.title: LAMB: Latent Multi-Hypothesis Beliefs for Long-Horizon Large Language Agents
items.summary: Long-horizon language agents require compact memories that retain interaction evidence while preserving competing hypotheses about unobserved states. Although effective, many belief-state methods encode memory in discrete natural language, where repeated compression can omit evidence or prematurely discard plausible alternatives. We introduce LAMB, a recurrent framework for latent multi-hypothesis beliefs. A Common--Delta factorization combines a shared Common state for interaction evidence with weighted Delta components for competing hypotheses. Relative evidence from action-outcome predictions guides recurrent hypothesis updates without generating textual memory. A context-conditioned readout exposes hypotheses separately to the policy through a fixed-token belief prefix in the default configuration. The belief modules and policy are jointly trained using action imitation and auxiliary state, outcome, and observation-discrimination objectives. Across ALFWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, LAMB matches or outperforms PABU, improving ALFWorld SR@30 and ScienceWorld success by 6.0 and 22.0 percentage points, respectively, and Crafter achievement progress by 26.37 points. On ALFWorld, it also reduces the redundant-action rate by 17.70 percentage points. These results support latent multi-hypothesis beliefs as compact memory for effective long-horizon decision making

items.title: SZED at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multi-Task Label-Attention and Cross-Modal Fusion for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection
items.summary: We present SZED's submission to ArGuard 2026 Track A: Arabic hateful meme detection. The task has two parts: binary classification (A1) and fine-grained multi-label tagging (A2). For A1, we fuse MARBERTv2 and CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings, comparing concatenation, self-attention, and ensemble heads. For A2, we use a multi-task label-attention architecture with per-class query vectors and an auxiliary head for cascade calibration. We reach macro-F1 = 0.7597 on A1 and 0.3142 on A2 (averaged over 10 active classes). We report reproducibility across runs, per-class error patterns, and the effect of cascade calibration on the long-tailed A2 label space.

items.title: Sharp Degree Bounds for Putinar Certificates in Terms of the Positivity Margin via Analytic Sums of Squares
items.summary: We establish sharp degree bounds for Putinar sum-of-squares (SOS) certificates in terms of the positivity margin $\delta$. For any fixed Archimedean quadratic module with prescribed generators and any fixed bound on the degree of the objective, we prove a uniform certificate-degree upper bound of $O(\delta^{-1/2}\log^2(2/\delta))$ for normalized polynomial objectives. We show that this bound is sharp by constructing a matching lower-bound example in three variables, thereby establishing that the dependence on $\delta$ is optimal. These matching bounds also yield sharp worst-case convergence rates for the Lasserre hierarchy.

items.title: Think Before You Transcribe: Context-Steered Reasoning for Hotword-Aware Speech Recognition
items.summary: Contextual automatic speech recognition (ASR) improves rare-entity recognition by supplying candidate hotwords, but retrieved candidates may be incomplete or incorrect. A reliable system must therefore exploit a relevant candidate without allowing unsupported alternatives to override the acoustic evidence. We propose a context-steered reasoning framework that generates a short, audio-grounded caption before transcription. This task-specific representation lets the model assess candidate relevance before making a lexical decision. Supervised fine-tuning establishes the structured caption-to-transcription behavior, while targeted trajectory injection strengthens group relative policy optimization when difficult utterances yield only unsuccessful rollouts. Experiments across diverse context conditions show that the proposed method consistently improves both transcription quality and hotword recognition while remaining robust to irrelevant candidates.

items.title: TRACE: Training-aware Robustness and Challenge Evaluation for Text-Vision Embedding Models
items.summary: Existing benchmarks for text-vision embedding models report aggregate scores that obscure whether performance comes from general capabilities, task-specific adaptation, or robustness to challenging tasks. We introduce TRACE, a Training-aware Robustness and Challenge Evaluation framework that reorganizes 168 tasks from various sources of datasets into three categories: General, Adaptability, and Challenge. Through controlled experiments on two text-vision embedding models, we show that combining general and adaptation data improves Adaptability performance by 7.67 and 7.09 points, respectively, while largely preserving General performance. However, Challenge performance remains below 5.0, with limited improvements from additional training data. Further analysis identifies multilingual and visual-document tasks as major weaknesses. Our findings demonstrate that data adaptation alone is insufficient to address these challenges, highlighting the need for methodological advances beyond data-centric improvements.

items.title: How to get the best and fairest performance out of your ASR system using activation steering
items.summary: Activation steering for ASR systems is an underexplored technique in improving both ASR performance and demographic fairness. We investigate two forms of activation steering: paired activation subtraction, and supervised optimization. We find the former to be ineffective at ameliorating ASR performance whatsoever, while the latter is quite effective at deriving steering vectors (SVs) that improve at once overall ASR performance and demographic fairness along such diverse axes as gender, age, and dialect. We also explore what types of data---from the most to the least personal---are necessary for calculating or training SVs. First, we show significant performance in performance from training SVs using an eclectic group of speakers from the same dataset. Furthermore, we find that vectors trained using acoustically similar speakers leads to ASR performances that are competitive or superior to vectors trained on the same speaker, or speakers from the same labeled demographic group. This finding shows that we can harness activation steering for few-shot adaptation given access to a speaker's demography, or zero-shot adaptation to unseen speakers without the need for any labels at all.

items.title: Evaluating Tibetan Speech Recognition Across Dialects and Adaptation Regimes: A Multi-Granularity Analysis
items.summary: Tibetan speech recognition is usually evaluated with character or syllable error rates because the writing system does not mark word boundaries. These metrics can rank systems differently and respond differently to adaptation failures. We combine character error rate, syllable error rate, and segmented word error rate in one evaluation framework. We use dictionary-based, neural, and language-model-based segmentation and compare their boundaries with expert annotations. We evaluate five ASR architectures on Lhasa Tibetan, then test zero-shot transfer and target-corpus adaptation on five additional corpus subsets. We also vary LoRA rank and training-data size to examine adaptation failure. The results show that a lower character error does not always lead to a lower syllable or segmented-word error. These ranking differences persist across corpora. Metric correlations also weaken in some unsuccessful adaptation settings. Higher LoRA ranks improve syllable and segmented-word scores but remain worse than full fine-tuning in the tested range. A standardized phonological representation provides another view of spelling errors. These findings support evaluation at several linguistic levels and motivate better segmentation and adaptation methods for low-resource ASR.

items.title: Decomposed Relation Extraction from Aviation Accident Narratives: Evaluating Transformer-Based Safety Knowledge Discovery under Relational Sparsity
items.summary: Relation extraction from aviation accident narratives is challenging because genuine safety relations are sparse among possible concept pairs. This study evaluates a decomposed framework separating relation classification from concept identification. A benchmark of 300 National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) narratives containing 2,524 unique concept-text nodes was expanded into 21,038 ordered candidate pairs, with only 248 (1.18%) representing RESULTS_IN or CONTRIBUTES_TO relations. A TF-IDF Linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) and weighted RoBERTa classifier were developed using an independent graph-annotated resource with hard-negative sampling and frozen before sealed evaluation. Development Macro-F1 scores of 0.4738 (SVM) and 0.4809 (RoBERTa) declined to 0.2741 and 0.2420 under exhaustive evaluation, with Matthews correlation coefficients of 0.0128 and 0.0197. False positives dominated: the SVM recovered 96 reference relations but generated 7,018 false positives, while RoBERTa recovered 125 but generated 9,824. Post-test diagnostics revealed overlapping RoBERTa confidence distributions and false positives even within valid relation-category directions. Complementary end-to-end SmolLM2 evaluation identified missed and unsupported relations alongside malformed outputs. These findings demonstrate that known concept endpoints do not guarantee reliable relation extraction and that sampled-negative development performance may poorly reflect exhaustive evaluation. Controlling false positives and managing candidate-space sparsity remain essential for aviation safety knowledge extraction.

items.title: Fluent but Fallible: Benchmarking Hallucination and Factual Reliability in Large Language Models
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced natural language processing and artificial intelligence applications through their capabilities in reasoning, text generation and knowledge retrieval. However, LLMs are still vulnerable to two important challenges: hallucination, generating factually incorrect or fabricated content, and response deviation, meaning systematic deviations from ground-truth responses. These limitations raise serious concerns regarding reliability and trustworthiness in academic and research environments. This study offers a thorough comparative analysis using a variety of metrics of ten advanced LLMs ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude~3.5~Sonnet, LLaMA~3, Mistral, Grok, Perplexity, DeepSeek~V3, Falcon, and Gemma based on a benchmark consisting of 70 carefully designed academic prompts across four complexity levels: Basic, Explanation, Advanced, and Tricky, evaluated in February 2025 on specific model versions. Each response was independently evaluated by three reviewers using five metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Response Deviation Index, and Hallucination Index. Perplexity and DeepSeek~V3 achieved the highest overall accuracy, while Gemini demonstrated strong recall and a well-balanced performance profile across all five metrics. LLaMA~3 showed strong resistance against hallucinations through a conservative method of generation. Advanced-level prompts proved most challenging across all models, while Tricky prompts were handled more reliably owing to their binary true/false structure. Falcon achieved perfect precision and zero hallucinations, but at the cost of the lowest recall and the highest response deviation. The results show a fundamental trade-off between response completeness and factual reliability, intensified by prompt complexity.

items.title: Cross-Lingual Reusability of LLM Pipelines: Financial Extraction, Multilingual Reasoning, and Semantic Screening
items.summary: Financial institutions increasingly deploy large language models (LLMs) in multilingual markets, raising a practical question: can pipelines developed and validated in English be reused across languages, or must they be rebuilt per locale? We test cross-lingual reusability along three dimensions--accuracy, reasoning-effort transfer, and behavioural stability--through three complementary tasks. Task 1 (cheque extraction) and Task 2 (Mintaka QA with pinned evidence across nine languages and nine model-effort configurations) test whether accuracy and effort settings transfer; Task 3 (FinanceBench pilot, 50 items over SEC 10-K filings in four languages) validates whether these patterns generalise to financial content. Accuracy reusability is broadly confirmed: Gemini 3.5 Flash achieves 95.2-97.6% extraction accuracy across prompt languages, and FinanceBench per-language means span 5.8pp (77.1-82.9%), though the language-difficulty ranking reverses between domains (Hindi is worst on Mintaka, best on FinanceBench at 82.9%). Effort reusability is domain-dependent: higher reasoning effort yields marginal gains on general-knowledge QA but up to 8pp on financial content, and effort configurations that help in English help proportionally in other languages. Behavioural reusability holds: citation-set overlap with English averages 77-79% Jaccard, with no single language consistently worse. Together, these results support qualified reuse of English-built pipelines, but per-domain, per-language validation remains necessary--neither semantic similarity nor self-reported confidence reliably predicts cross-lingual accuracy.

items.title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
items.summary: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. A model trained on MIMIC-III with a closed-vocabulary tokenizer can use only 13% of eICU events. We introduce MEDIATOR, a discrete ontology-agnostic tokenizer that maps any clinical concept expressed as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, turning EHR harmonization into open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or a fixed vocabulary. Trained with synonym supervision and guided by enriched concept descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs, MEDIATOR collapses equivalent expressions while organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. Used as the token interface of an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves mean AUPRC over the strongest prior tokenizer by 4.0 points (8% relative) on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and by 8.6 points (29% relative) in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, where it uses all events. The transfer gain combines coverage and representation, as MEDIATOR remains the best tokenizer under identical inputs (+1.0 and +1.9 points on operational and subcohort-mortality tasks). Same-encoder controls show that the text encoder drives in-domain accuracy, while the learned objectives of MEDIATOR drive transfer robustness and entity-linking quality. MEDIATOR also enables transferable attribution across hospitals.

items.title: Joint Constraint Aggregation for Qualifier-Sensitive Retrieval-Augmented QA
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented QA can fail even when the correct answer is in the retrieved evidence. This can happen when a competing answer satisfies some, but not all, of the question's requirements and is mentioned frequently in the retrieved documents, which can make it appear to be the best-supported answer. To test whether this retrieval skew actually affects the decision, we manipulate it directly: increasing the prevalence of passages that favor the competing answer makes the model more likely to select it. This points to a decision problem that candidate-level support alone cannot resolve. We therefore introduce Joint Constraint Aggregation (JCA), which compares candidates against the same question-derived requirements using the retrieved evidence. Across three evaluation settings and three instruction-tuned backbones, JCA improves overall accuracy, and its advantage grows when retrieval favors a competing answer. Together, these results suggest that when partial matches and retrieval prominence pull models toward a competing answer, comparing candidates against the question's full requirements can make selection more reliable.

items.title: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
items.summary: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. Existing methods compute similarity using cosine distance over either the model's hidden states or gradients. However, we observe that this max-similarity strategy induces a mode-seeking bias: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. To address this, we propose ICLHerd, a data selection framework that leverages the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging. We further introduce in-context learning as a validation proxy, enabling efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Results show that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms, highlighting the importance of balancing mode-seeking and mode-averaging.

items.title: GRID: Modeling Health Influencer Discourse as Argument Networks for Credibility Assessment
items.summary: Health-related discussions on social media are increasingly shaped by influencers who offer diverse, and often competing perspectives on the same issue. Yet, such content is typically evaluated in isolation, without considering the broader discourse in which it appears. We introduce GRID (Grounded Reasoning over Interconnected Discourse), a framework for evaluating influencer content through collective inference over the surrounding discourse. GRID represents each video as an argumentation graph connecting claims to its central message, or takeaway, links related claims and takeaways across videos, grounds claims in scientific evidence, and jointly infers credibility over the resulting network. We evaluate GRID on an end-to-end health-related content validation task using 569 influencer videos grounded in expert assessments. Our results show that accounting for the broader discourse improves influencer content validation. Finally, we use GRID-inferred credibility to demonstrate how argumentative strategies and moral framing differ between low- and high-credibility content.

items.title: SITO: Sifting a Commercial Text-Safety API for Missed Harm and False Flags in English, Ukrainian and Surzhyk
items.summary: Platforms that host young users screen messages with commercial text-safety APIs, but independent evidence on how often such systems miss harm or flag harmless text is scarce, especially outside English, and the documentation of the one studied here leaves its false-positive rate unquantified. We evaluated one such API, Tuteliq Detect as deployed under the release identifier tuteliq-detect-v5.20261011 (not the separately published v6 model), on six harm categories: authorised push-payment fraud, money-mule recruitment, social engineering, romance scams, gambling harm and bullying. We built SITO (Synthetic Independent Text-safety benchmark with Overflagging tests; sito is Ukrainian for 'sieve'), 2,332 synthetic cases in English, Ukrainian and mixed Ukrainian, with each harmful case matched by hard harmless ones: same-topic messages, minimal-edit contrasts, warnings and retrospective accounts. On English text the system flagged 84.9-94.1% of harmful cases and 0-4.3% of harmless ones per category. It missed third-party reports of ongoing harm far more often than perpetrators' messages (63.6% against 95.1% recall, all languages), when sent without the settings the API offers for reports of harm. Ukrainian and mixed-language input was detected at least as often as English, recall was lower on text from a held-out generator family, so headline recall may be optimistic, and 3.2% of cases received a different decision in repeated runs. A platform should measure false positives on its own traffic and check how bystander reports are handled. The datasets, generation prompts and code are released.

items.title: On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models
items.summary: Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.

items.title: Preference-Aware Pareto Steering for Multi-Task Speech LLMs
items.summary: Speech large language models (LLMs) perform multiple tasks, including automatic speech recognition (ASR), timestamp prediction (TS), and speech translation (ST). Joint training of speech LLMs creates task trade-offs, yet standard training with fixed loss weights does not generally control the resulting trade-off according to deployment preferences. To address this, we propose Endpoint-Anchored Preference-Aware Sampling Uniformly along the Pareto Front (EA-SURF), an a priori method that adapts scalarization weights so that the resulting task trade-off reflects the desired preference. EA-SURF retains the standard weighted-loss training pipeline, tracking the current model's performance relative to each task-specific reference and adapting the scalarization weights as training proceeds. We theoretically show that EA-SURF can match a desired preference, with the update becoming stationary at the target under checkable regularity conditions. Across six three-objective speech LLM requests, EA-SURF empirically converges toward the requested targets and increases endpoint-inclusive normalized hypervolume by 17.8% over fixed loss weighting.

items.title: The Culture Within: Towards Mechanistic Understanding of Cultural Reasoning in LLMs
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate across culturally diverse settings, yet existing evaluations largely measure cultural behavior at the output level. We introduce CultureLens, a reference-grounded benchmark and mechanistic study of how LLMs use cultural information. CultureLens contains 9,261 scenarios across 75 countries and systematically varies country, value, true-norm, and contradictory-norm evidence. Across Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B, and Qwen-3.5-27B, stating a contradictory norm lowers aligned answers by 32-47 percentage points, even when the model answers correctly from the country alone. Mechanistically, models default to Anglophone norms when no country is given. The failure under a contradictory norm is not one of missing knowledge, as blocking the norm inside the model restores the correct answer in most cases. Models accept a stated norm according to how it is presented and not whether it is true, which leaves them most exposed to errors in retrieved content. Supervised fine-tuning with contradictory-norm examples raises aligned answers under a contradictory norm to 85-93%, including on unseen countries, at a small cost under a true norm.

items.title: LoWAgent: A Low-Resource Multilingual Benchmark for Web Agents
items.summary: Web agents are typically evaluated on English-language interfaces, leaving their ability to operate across the world's multilingual websites largely unexplored. This gap is especially significant for low-resource languages, where standardized resources for evaluating web agents remain limited. To address this gap, we introduce Low-Resource Web Agent Benchmark (LoWAgent), a benchmark for evaluating web agents across different low-resource languages (LRLs) in comparison to the default, English. LoWAgent evaluates web agents across English and four LRLs: Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, and Amharic. The benchmark comprises of six fully localized websites, instantiated across five languages to yield 3,000 task instances. We evaluate three closed-source and five open-source models across all five languages on all six websites. Our findings show that both closed-source and open-source models experience performance degradation for LRLs compared to English, with substantially greater performance drops observed among the open-source model agents. We further evaluate the robustness of the models on realistic interface disruptions, such as cookie notices and advertisement pop-ups, and find that these further degrade agentic performance. Finally, we show that post-training on a small subset of LoWAgent traces can significantly improve low-resource language agentic task performance, demonstrating the usefulness of our benchmark.

items.title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams
items.summary: Cooperative language-model agents can improve without weight updates by revising reusable skills, but only if a shared team reward is traced to the responsible agent and skill. Existing methods credit the skills present in each trajectory, yet presence is not responsibility: a harmful skill active in successful runs still earns positive credit. We present \textbf{GRSE}, \textbf{G}roup-\textbf{R}elative \textbf{S}kill \textbf{E}volution, which assigns behavioral credit by comparison: inspired by GRPO, it executes each question several times under the same skill libraries and contrasts the executions to credit agent--skill pairs, with structured diagnosis of failures. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills, the closest prior method, on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions ($+6.7$ and $+3.2$ F1). Its gains rest on better-grounded retrieval rather than answers given without evidence, and its learned skills transfer between the multi-hop tasks. GRSE is robust to corrupted libraries: starting from planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and recovers the score of a clean library ($+6.3$ points), whereas MASkills misattributes two and falls below its starting point.

items.title: MMedAgent-Plus: Scaling Multimodal Medical Agents across Modalities, Tasks and Workflows
items.summary: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).

items.title: CEFR-oriented Russian Text Simplification Using Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: We present a study on controlled automatic simplification of Russian texts using preference-based optimization algorithms with a focus on adapting texts to the A1, A2 and B1 proficiency levels. We fine-tune YandexGPT using Rejection Sampling and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) methods to improve control over the complexity of the generated text. We compare several training configurations that differ in dataset composition, text type and the strategy used to construct preference pairs for DPO. For automatic evaluation we train a regression model based on ruRoBERTa-large to predict continuous complexity scores corresponding to CEFR levels. We also consider semantic similarity, lexical coverage and quantitative readability metrics. Human evaluation assesses simplicity, fluency and adequacy. Our best model achieves 87.15\% target level accuracy, an MAE of 0.35 CEFR levels and a target interval MAE of 0.11. items.title: Predicting Linear Relational Decodability Without the Relation
items.summary: Linear relational embeddings (LREs) approximate a language model's subject-to-object mapping with an affine function. Their faithfulness varies enormously across relations, from near zero for person_father to the ceiling for country_capital_city. We investigate the factors that contribute to this variation and demonstrate that it can be significantly predicted from a readout that is not aware of the underlying relation. To do so, we propose a novel form of the Jacobian lens, the entity lens. Whereas the Jacobian lens is estimated across all tokens and concepts, the entity lens EL_t is trained to predict what the model will output for an entity of type t under the neutral prompt "{} is known for"; e.g., we train ELs for countries and persons. After estimating an entity lens, we measure how highly it ranks the model's answer for a relation without using any relation-specific information in estimation and prediction. Across 28 relations of the LRE dataset on Olmo-3-7B this relation-agnostic score correlates with LRE faithfulness at \rho = 0.7355 (p < .01). This suggests that linear decodability is largely a property of what a subject's representation already carries, rather than of the relation being decoded. Moving the unit of analysis from the relation to the individual fact, we conclude that new relation datasets and analysis methods are needed to address several problems in existing datasets, most prominently semantically weak first tokens (e.g., most predicted universities' first token is "University") and reference competition (e.g., the LLM confuses obscure actor names with competing non-actor entities that have the same last name). Our full pipeline is available at https://github.com/jonasrohw/entity-lens

items.title: Diagnostic Analysis for Large Language Model Reasoning
items.summary: Reasoning structures (e.g., chains and graphs) are increasingly used for probabilistic inference, factuality verification, and uncertainty estimation, but their structural reliability is rarely evaluated directly. We test whether this reliability holds through a proposed two-stage diagnostic evaluation in open-ended multi-hop QA. Stage 1 tests different capabilities required to construct reasoning graphs, showing that graph reliability varies with topology, prompt design, and model family. Stage 2 uses uncertainty estimation as a downstream test case. Generated-edge experiments show that graph-based computation is sensitive to upstream graph errors, with performance dropping relative to the gold-graph setting. Gold-graph experiments further show that graph structure provides little benefit when used only as prompt context, but improves the separation of correct from incorrect answers by confidence score and enables node-level diagnostics.

items.title: Target-Aware Curation of Hallucination Stress Tests for Large Language Models
items.summary: Hallucination stress tests can yield similar average scores across language models even when different prompts elicit hallucinations in each model. We develop a procedure that iteratively edits source-grounded seed prompts to expose hallucinations in a target model. An LLM editor revises each prompt in response to the target's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation. In the main setting, the target also receives feedback on its previous response. Experiments cover 500 seeds from seven datasets and ten topics, with intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations evaluated across open-weight and closed-source models. Editing substantially increases judge-rated severity over the seeds. In the baseline configuration, retained responses fall in the judge's strong-hallucination bin in 77.2% of runs targeting extrinsic hallucination and 74.2% targeting intrinsic hallucination. Later editing rounds account for more than half of the mean score increase. Among 219 prompts that pass model-assisted source-validity checks, 89 elicit responses containing unsupported claims. Across five models, 200 curated prompts yield similar average severity scores, although pairwise Spearman correlations between prompt-level scores are only $\rho=0.0387$ to $0.1897$. Curated prompts can be reused across models, but their diagnostic value depends on source validity and the failures they expose in each model.

items.title: Auditing Safety Preference Supervision with Recorded Derivations
items.summary: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, we train one policy model with direct preference optimization across five training seeds. Mean measured benign refusal is 40.82 percent on 1,319 benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones, and mean measured toxic refusal is 84.98 percent on 655 toxic prompts. This study distinguishes the reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness. The recorded derivations make preference construction open to inspection, while attribute correctness and semantic safety require separate validation.

items.title: African Languages AI Safety Readiness Report
items.summary: With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) across languages and domains, AI safety has emerged as a critical global concern. However, due to resource constraints, research and development efforts tend to prioritize a limited number of high-resource languages, leaving many others, especially those spoken in Africa, underrepresented. While existing research on language "resource-ness" has largely examined whether sufficient resources are available to develop language technologies, the question of whether languages are adequately represented in AI safety research has received attention only more recently. This report examines the readiness of African languages for inclusion in AI safety discussions, drawing on existing literature and data. It considers four factors: the availability of AI-relevant resources, including text data; national AI policy support; performance on established text benchmarks; and speaker population. Based on these factors, languages are grouped into four readiness categories: fully ready, mostly ready, emerging, and foundational support needed. This classification is intended to inform the inclusion of African languages in AI safety benchmarks, highlight varying levels of preparedness, and guide strategic investment in data development, policy, and community engagement for underrepresented languages.

items.title: When Does Hate Transfer? A Large-Scale Study of Cross-Lingual Hate Speech Detection
items.summary: Effective detection of hate content is essential for maintaining healthy online communities, yet performance can vary substantially across languages. This work investigates a core practical question: Can training data from one language support hate-speech detection in another language with comparable performance? To answer this question, we conduct a large-scale study across 14 languages. \change{We observe consistent patterns in which certain language pairs transfer more effectively than others. Among the factors we measure, linguistic similarity is the strongest predictor of these patterns, with temporal overlap and dataset-size difference playing smaller roles. These measurable factors do not fully explain the observed patterns; a complementary qualitative analysis suggests that shared cultural cues and communicative norms may be associated with some of the remaining cases, particularly within several clusters. We present this cultural interpretation as a hypothesis from qualitative inspection rather than a measured cause.}{} Our analysis includes low-resource languages, offering practical insights into when cross-lingual transfer can support them and where its limitations emerge. These findings inform the design of more reliable multilingual hate-detection systems.

items.title: RealControlBench: A Benchmark for Interpretability-Informed Fine-Grained Control of LLMs and Agents
items.summary: Existing steering benchmarks are built around simplified, isolated generation tasks and evaluate a single behavioral attribute under controlled settings that do not reflect the diversity and complexity of practical deployment. As a result, performance on these benchmarks provides only a limited picture of how steering methods perform in the real world. We therefore introduce RealControlBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating fine-grained steering of LLMs and LLM agents across diverse behavioral targets and interaction settings. RealControlBench extends steering evaluation beyond isolated generations to complex, execution-grounded, multi-turn agent interactions, covering five complementary dimensions: instruction-following control, agentic tool-use decision control, reasoning-performance steering, reasoning-length control, and trajectory-conditioned safety awareness. Rather than measuring steering success alone, the benchmark jointly evaluates target controllability and capability preservation, including instruction following, reasoning performance, and downstream agent utility and safety. It further examines whether steering effects remain specific and robust across prompt variations, domains, and model architectures. Our evaluation shows that existing steering methods remain unreliable across realistic control objectives: they often fail to consistently induce the intended behavior and can substantially degrade the model's underlying task performance. These results suggest that strong steering effects in controlled settings do not necessarily translate into reliable control in more realistic evaluations. By providing a unified, model-agnostic steering evaluation framework, RealControlBench aims to support the development of steering methods that are not only effective but also precise, robust, and useful in realistic AI deployments.
