items.title: Region-Specific EEG Classification of Hypnotic Susceptibility Using a Sliding-Window 2D CNN: A Subject-Independent Evaluation
items.summary: We investigate whether a 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on minimally preprocessed EEG signals can classify hypnotic susceptibility across distinct brain regions. Sixty-two male participants (32 Control, 30 Guided Imagery / Hipno group) underwent a 20-minute EEG recording using a 256-channel EGI cap. A sliding-window approach evaluates all 10-second windows within the recording for each of seven predefined brain regions (prefrontal, frontal, temporal, central, parietal, occipital, and facial), yielding up to 868 independently trained models. Initial screening with a segment-level 90/10 random split showed that five regions exceeded the 0.67 accuracy threshold, with the occipital region achieving the highest mean accuracy (0.721) across 90.3% of windows. Subject-independent evaluation via Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation, however, substantially revised this picture: occipital performance collapsed to near-chance (mean ACC 0.453, AUC 0.429), revealing that high random-split accuracy was driven by subject-specific EEG fingerprints rather than genuine group differences. In contrast, the frontal and prefrontal regions maintained above-chance LOSO accuracy (0.646 and 0.624, respectively), demonstrating genuine generalisability. These results underscore the necessity of subject-independent validation in EEG-based classification studies and highlight anterior cortical regions as more reliable neural markers of hypnotic susceptibility.

items.title: Do Neural Models Prefer Their Submodels?
items.summary: A neural model is the set of functions that can be expressed by a given neural network architecture. Neural models contain natural submodels, such as those obtained by setting some neurons to be inactive. We study the geometry of neural models and ask whether they prefer their submodels. By this we mean whether local minimizers of the loss function lie in a given submodel. We introduce a geometric framework to determine if this occurs. For shallow multilayer perceptrons, we show that subnetworks with inactive hidden neurons are never preferred. For deep multilayer perceptrons, we give conditions under which subnetworks with inactive hidden neurons are not preferred. For lightning self-attention, lower-rank submodels are usually not preferred, but we identify examples where they are because they lie on a boundary of the model. Our results show that, aside from a few exceptions, preference for submodels cannot be explained by the geometry of the neural model, and must instead come from other sources such as training dynamics.

items.title: CNN-based classifier for subject-independent MBTI Extraversion/Introversion preference classification from short-time EEG signals
items.summary: This study examines whether short, minimally preprocessed EEG segments contain sufficient information to distinguish between individuals classified as extraverted or introverted according to the Myers--Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI). EEG recordings from 50 participants were divided into 4-s segments and analyzed using a subject-independent nested 5-fold cross-validation procedure to compare EEGNet, EEGProgress, and a newly proposed compact convolutional architecture, SSCNet. SSCNet achieved the highest mean accuracy (0.6481), AUC (0.7063), and F1-score (0.6276). The proposed architecture also showed the lowest variability across folds. SSCNet demonstrated the best computational efficiency, with the shortest median training epoch time and the highest training throughput despite having a similar number of trainable parameters to EEGProgress. The results suggest that MBTI Extraversion--Introversion preferences may be moderately predictable from short time-domain EEG segments without manual spectral feature extraction, while highlighting the importance of subject-independent validation and computationally efficient model design.

arXiv:2610.28442v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study examines whether short, minimally preprocessed EEG segments contain sufficient information to distinguish between individuals classified as extraverted or introverted according to the Myers--Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI). EEG recordings from 50 participants were divided into 4-s segments and analyzed using a subject-independent nested 5-fold cross-validation procedure to compare EEGNet, EEGProgress, and a newly proposed compact convolutional architecture, SSCNet. SSCNet achieved the highest mean accuracy (0.6481), AUC (0.7063), and F1-score (0.6276). The proposed architecture also showed the lowest variability across folds. SSCNet demonstrated the best computational efficiency, with the shortest median training epoch time and the highest training throughput despite having a similar number of trainable parameters to EEGProgress. The results suggest that MBTI Extraversion--Introversion preferences may be moderately predictable from short time-domain EEG segments without manual spectral feature extraction, while highlighting the importance of subject-independent validation and computationally efficient model design.

items.title: LocaLeJEPA: Maximum Entropy Representations under Geometric Priors
items.summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) offer an appealing approach to self-supervised learning, but are typically prone to representation collapse. LeJEPA resolves this by introducing a theoretically grounded distribution-matching objective that drives the embedding towards an isotropic Gaussian. However, this approach is fundamentally tied to Euclidean assumptions, and its global target does not reflect domain-specific geometric priors, such as the use of non-Euclidean embedding geometries, e.g., equivariant CNNs or hyperbolic ViTs. We thus introduce LocaLeJEPA, a framework motivated by a manifold-theoretic reformulation of LeJEPA's entropy-maximization property. The accompanying LocaLeReg, a novel locally Euclidean distribution-matching regularizer, enables a stable and scalable implementation of the LocaLeJEPA framework. We then perform extensive experiments in the vision setting on models trained on ImageNet-1K. LocaLeJEPA significantly outperforms LeJEPA when paired with hyperbolic ViT-S/8 and equivariant ResNet-50 backbones, and also with ordinary Euclidean ViT-S/8 and ViT-L/14 backbones. This holds both in terms of linear and k-NN classification performance on ImageNet and on a series of downstream tasks tested. We view the LocaLeJEPA formalism as a principled approach to the JEPA paradigm that better respects intrinsic data geometry while also accommodating generalizations to exotic embedding geometries. Code available at https://github.com/alessioborgi/LocaLeJEPA.

items.title: Geometry-Agnostic Data-Driven Discovery of Extreme Scenarios
items.summary: We introduce a two-stage data-driven neural framework for discovering dynamically admissible extreme scenarios. Rather than assuming prior knowledge of the governing equations, the first stage infers the effective dynamical constraints directly from observational data. When the underlying physical system possesses suitable symmetries, the learned dynamics can be represented in a geometry-agnostic form, independent of any fixed grid, coordinate system, dimensionality, and intrinsic curvature. In the second stage, a physics-informed neural-search uses this learned dynamics to uncover rare, high-impact coherent structures that may not have appeared in the original observations. We demonstrate this framework through representative examples of increasing dimensionality and geometric complexity. Starting from a traditionally learned Duffing dynamics, we find a homoclinic pulse as a plausible localized extreme scenario. Next, since the same equation also appears in the stationary nonlinear Schrodinger system, with the coordinate interpreted as space instead of time, this pulse becomes a standing soliton. We then retrain the first stage using a geometry-agnostic neural representation, enabling the learned dynamics to be lifted to higher-dimensional space to obtain higher-dimensional solitary profile, known as Townes soliton. Finally, with a Liouville system, we demonstrate that dynamics learned from data on a (1+1)-dimensional Lorentzian quasi-manifold can be transferred to a (2+0)-dimensional Euclidean manifold to identify an instanton. Our approach can be applied to other coherent spatiotemporal structures, including kinks, rogue waves, compactons, peakons, and potentially even singularities, with applications in risk analysis, nonlinear forecasting, and anomaly detection.

items.title: Model- and Layer-Level Closed-Loop Forecasting with SSM-Based Spiking Neural Networks
items.summary: Deep State-Space Models (Deep SSMs) have shown promising performance and computational benefits in processing of time-series data with complex temporal dependencies. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) constitute a biologically inspired class of deep SSMs, where computing blocks communicate through spikes, discrete single-bit events rather than continuous activation functions. A particularly important task in time-series processing is forecasting, i.e. predicting future values of a sequence from past observations alone. However, how to best perform forecasting with SNNs is an open question, where the standard autoregressive nature of the data processing with SNNs requires values that are not available during the forecasting phase. In this article, we address this challenge. We explore two closed-loop forecasting strategies, in which the network's own generated values are fed back into the network as if they were observed past values: (i) model-level and (ii) layer-level closed-loop forecasting. We evaluate these approaches on the ETT-small datasets, a standard benchmark for time-series forecasting, under both spike-based and continuous activation functions. We compare the proposed closed-loop approaches against state-of-the-art methods such as SpaceTime, as well as the zero-masking baseline in S4. Both of the proposed approaches perform comparably to or better than zero-masking with S4, and in most cases match SpaceTime. These findings highlight the trade-off between continuous and low-bit quantized activations, and demonstrate that the proposed Deep SSM architectures provide a competitive framework for forecasting.

items.title: Present but Hard to Read: Probing Latent Reasoning with Minimal Pairs
items.summary: Probing studies of latent reasoning often read a model's state where the answer begins and take a failed probe as evidence that a value is absent. We test this with a digit copied from the question, in the looped model Ouro-1.4B and the standard transformer Qwen2.5-1.5B. Comparing prompts that differ only in that digit shows it is present at the last prompt token, in a code shared across questions (readout about 0.9). A probe that sees one prompt at a time, the usual setting, barely reads it: 0.36 in Ouro and 0.19 in Qwen even after 5,249 training questions. The digit's change is small rather than crowded: random noise lands on equally busy directions, while a random word in its place moves the state far more and is readable. Since every varied token leaves a trace, a successful probe is ambiguous too. We give a protocol, including a synthetic null for generic mixing, for testing computed values against copies and mixtures of the inputs. In pre-registered studies of two-step problems it finds a small signal for the unwritten intermediate a+b just before Ouro writes the answer's last digit, and its sign follows the operation, though mixing alone produces much of that sign-following part. Holding that value at another problem's from the first loop on does not move the written digit toward the other problem's, while the same patch of the answer does: the value is readable but not used.

items.title: ECG for laboratory values:A comprehensive physiological and technical analysis
items.summary: Laboratory measurements are essential for clinical decision making but typically require invasive blood sampling. Recent research suggests that ECG recordings may contain information beyond cardiac rhythm and provide information related to laboratory values. This thesis investigates NT-proBNP prediction from ECG recordings and patient metadata using a multimodal deep learning framework, while considering the physiological plausibility of ECG-based prediction. It also compares a 1-lead configuration using lead II with the corresponding 12-lead configuration. Additional experiments on glucose, hemoglobin, and potassium are presented in the appendix. Regression, binary classification, and three-class classification experiments were conducted using MIMIC-IV, with the three-class task based on clinically established thresholds. The 12-lead configuration consistently achieved better performance. Regression reached a mean absolute error of 534.98 pg/mL for 1-lead and 514.27 pg/mL for 12-lead. Binary classification achieved AUROCs of 0.849 and 0.876, respectively, while three-class classification achieved macro-averaged AUROCs of 0.738 and 0.752. The results indicate that precise NT-proBNP regression remains challenging, whereas broader concentration ranges can be classified more effectively. The findings are consistent with the physiological hypothesis that ECG characteristics and NT-proBNP concentrations reflect shared cardiovascular processes. ECG-based NT-proBNP prediction may therefore provide complementary information, particularly for classifying broader concentration ranges. However, laboratory measurements remain necessary, and validation on independent datasets is required.

items.title: GraphCast-Mamba: Learning Non-Markovian Corrections for Weather Forecasting
items.summary: Unresolved atmospheric processes can introduce history dependence beyond the short input windows used by many weather forecasting models. We introduce GraphCast--Mamba, which augments a frozen, pretrained $1^\circ$ GraphCast backbone with a trainable Mamba correction branch combining graph message passing and Mamba layers. The branch retains a temporal memory state across successive six-hour forecast steps, learning corrections informed by temporal context beyond GraphCast's two-frame input. Training is confined to the correction branch, using ERA5 data from 2015--2021. After 2,500 optimizer updates, including warm-up, the selected model achieves substantial improvements relative to the uncorrected GraphCast backbone. It reduces the GraphCast loss (normalized weighted mean-squared error; MSE) by 14.42% when aggregated over the full ten-day forecast and by 21.66% at day 10 (240 h after forecast initialization). At this final forecast lead time, root-mean-square error (RMSE) decreases by 7.09--14.60% across all 11 evaluated variable groups, spanning temperature, wind, pressure, geopotential, specific humidity, and precipitation. These results demonstrate broad improvements in ten-day weather forecasts through a short correction-training schedule while retaining the pretrained backbone.

items.title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks
items.summary: Discrete diffusion models iteratively denoise a noisy sequence of categorical data such as text, enabling any-order generation with self-correction and in-filling capabilities. This makes them promising candidates for reasoning, planning, and constrained-generation tasks like coding and math. Yet masked and uniform diffusion erase a token's identity in a single corruption event, so their noisy states cannot explicitly represent partially resolved uncertainty in which several alternatives remain plausible. We close this gap with Binary Discrete Diffusion, a family of continuous-time discrete-diffusion processes whose noisy state is a set of candidate tokens per position, represented as a binary membership vector. Binary diffusion changes candidate sets through additions and removals, allowing information to be lost and recovered gradually while the diffusion state itself represents partial uncertainty. On Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban, and graph coloring, the symmetric formulation of binary diffusion consistently outperforms strong, well-tuned masked and uniform baselines under matched architectures and controlled training, sampling, and tuning budgets, with its largest gains on the hardest instances, while remaining competitive on language modeling (Text8, TinyStories, OpenWebText). These results support candidate sets as an effective intermediate representation for iterative reasoning and show that the corruption kernel can materially change the computation learned by the reverse model.

items.title: Discount Yourself: Self-inclusive Freshness-weighted Gossip for Decentralised Learning under Client Outages
items.summary: Decentralised federated learning (DFL) trains personalised models on devices that average with their neighbours rather than with a central server. Real devices, however, are often offline for hours or days, and a client returning from an outage can recover only by aggregating the models its neighbourhood holds. We observe that the stalest of these models is usually the client's own, a case that existing staleness-aware rules, which discount only the models a client receives, do not address. We formalise aggregation after an outage as estimating the state of a fully available network and derive three principles. First, the receiver must be discounted like any neighbour. Every rule that weights it at least as much as each neighbour has an error that grows without bound with the outage, whereas discounting all candidates by relative staleness keeps the error bounded. Second, staleness must be measured as inherited lag rather than age, since local training resets a model's age but not the lag it absorbed from stale neighbours. We introduce the effective lag, which tracks this quantity at the cost of one scalar per message. Third, the discount must be steep, because absorbed lag persists in every later round. These principles define Self-inclusive Freshness-weighted Gossip (SFG), a family of drop-in aggregation rules with the communication and computation of decentralised federated averaging, whose guarantees hold for the stale receiver itself. On three image benchmarks and eight outage processes, including real smartphone availability traces, the lag-based members SFG-L and SFG-Cut consistently outperform decentralised federated averaging and recent age-of-information rules, and ablations show that each principle is necessary. The analysis also explains why tuned limited merging from gossip learning is effective.

items.title: Learning Computational Structure for Sample-Efficient Prediction
items.summary: Statistical learning in high dimensions suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Fortunately, many functions of practical interest are compositionally sparse, meaning they admit a composition of local functions, each depending on only a few variables, allowing sample complexity to depend on local arity rather than ambient dimension. Yet realizing this benefit requires exploiting hidden compositional structure, which theory does not establish for practical gradient-based training. We study this gap with CSFRBench, a controlled benchmark that hides the target's compositional computation during training but retains it for diagnosis, and find that dense networks and sparsity-based baselines leave much of that benefit unrealized. Inspired by the spatial organization of biological neural circuits, we introduce Learned Wiring (LeWi): each neuron has a learned low-dimensional embedding, only nearby neurons connect, and embeddings and weights are trained jointly. LeWi improves sample efficiency on targets with hierarchical structure, intermediate reuse, or independent modules. Across 32 additional targets generated by independently sampled computation graphs, LeWi is the most sample-efficient method not given the target graph, with 27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks. Dense networks perform better on targets with a single high-arity function. LeWi's representations and connectivity align with the target computation. On 17 world-model prediction tasks spanning control, navigation, and manipulation, LeWi beats the dense baseline on 16 and wins 99/119 baseline comparisons. These results show that jointly learning connectivity and weights can exploit computational structure to improve sample efficiency.

items.title: When Do LLMs Help with Feature Selection? A Systematic Empirical Study
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can leverage semantic feature names alongside summary statistics for tabular feature selection, yet it remains unclear when such information improves subset selection relative to established statistical methods. We investigate this question within an 18-dataset framework comprising 10 datasets for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training, 2 for checkpoint validation, and 6 held-out evaluation datasets. We compare five classical baselines, frozen Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.3-70B selectors, and two GRPO-adapted Qwen2.5-7B models, reporting classification ROC-AUC and regression R^2 separately and using dataset-wise ranks for cross-task comparison. Across five seeded evaluation partitions, classical selectors generally achieve higher predictive performance than the tested 7B LLM/RL selectors, including under a pre-specified ~33% feature budget with strict train-only classical fitting, while the 7B selectors retain compact subsets. A cardinality-matched semantic sensitivity experiment shows that, for Zero-shot Qwen-7B, informative feature names improve regression performance over anonymized and shuffled alternatives (+0.1964 and +0.1606 mean R^2), whereas aggregate classification differences are smaller (+0.0159 and +0.0084 ROC-AUC) and dataset-dependent. These results characterize when semantic information benefits LLM-based feature selection and show that classical selectors remain strong baselines for predictive tabular feature selection.

items.title: Convergence of stochastic gradient descent for learning linear neural networks
items.summary: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is the cornerstone of modern deep learning, yet its theoretical convergence properties remain poorly understood in non-convex settings. To address this gap, we study SGD dynamics in deep linear neural networks - simplified models that retain key non-convex characteristics while remaining analytically tractable. Building on recent results for gradient descent, we extend convergence guarantees to SGD under regularized squared loss. We establish almost sure boundedness of SGD iterates. Using the framework of asymptotic pseudotrajectories from stochastic approximation theory, our analysis establishes then, for both deterministic and adaptive step-size choices, convergence of SGD to the set of critical points under mild conditions (without relying on Lipschitz properties or whitened data). To our knowledge, this is the first work providing almost sure convergence guarantees for SGD in deep linear networks, bridging the gap between theoretical optimization and practical stochastic training.

items.title: Asymmetric Bidirectional Predictive Dynamics in Google Search and COVID-19 Time Series: A Multi-Horizon Forecast-Error Analysis
items.summary: Online search activity is widely used as a digital trace of information seeking during epidemics, but its predictive value is often reduced to correlation, a selected lag, or a single forecast-error score. We examine eight pre-specified Google Trends-COVID-19 pairs in both directions using matched LightGBM forecasts over rolling 400-day windows and horizons of 1-14 days. Log-RMSE gain is combined with forecast-error distribution entropy (FEDE), which captures horizon-dependent changes in the signed error distribution. The resulting directional predictive signature comprises response class, RMSE effect, FEDE endpoint and early-slope responses, persistence across rolling regimes, and horizon profile. For screening candidate directions, we also introduce a relative persistence-weighted directional predictive response strength (DPRS) on a within-study 0-100 scale; 100 denotes the strongest observed response in the comparison set, not an absolute coupling maximum. The pairs show concordant, RMSE-only, FEDE-only, and mixed responses. "loss of smell" -> reported cases is accuracy-dominant, with mean log-RMSE gain 0.104 (about 9.9% equivalent RMSE reduction) and DPRS 100, whereas the reverse direction is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.048; DPRS=42). "covid test" -> positive rate is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.039; positive in 72% of windows; DPRS=98) despite negative RMSE gain, while "lockdown" -> stringency is the clearest concordant case (DPRS=78). World-level symptom/case pairs are less persistent. Thus, forecast accuracy and error-distribution dynamics are complementary, predictive effects can be direction- and metric-dependent, and forecast horizon is part of the relationship. Aggregated regime-level patterns should not be extrapolated to individual time points or interpreted as evidence of causality.

items.title: The Dynamics of Collapse and Recovery in Clustered Federated Learning
items.summary: Clustered federated learning (CFL) can suffer from cluster collapse. In particular, under unfavorable initialization, early client assignments concentrate heterogeneous groups on one cluster model, which is then trained toward a pooled compromise, while another model receives no updates. Since the current models determine client routing and routing determines subsequent model updates, we formulate clustered federated learning as control of an unknown dynamical system, with cluster models as the evolving state, client routing patterns as the control input, and routing interventions as state dependent controllers. In a two group linear model, we identify an initialization region in which greedy routing makes collapse self reinforcing. We then derive finite horizon error dynamics showing how routing interventions can reverse collapse by repeatedly training the starved model, primarily with updates from its compatible group. Motivated by this condition, each client uses blocked EXP3 to choose between greedy routing and interventions that redirect updates toward unused models. Experiments show that with simpler predictors and faster specialist formation, autonomous controller selection recovers usable specialists from unfavorable starts that trap standard CFL baselines. In transformed FEMNIST, the synchronized-entry configuration with persistent commitment recovers usable specialists in settings where the autonomous controller configuration often does not. Code and scripts for reproducing the experiments and figures are available at https://github.com/prsinha1/FedRecover.

items.title: The Token-Energy Law of LLM Decode: Active Bytes and Realized Time Account for Joules per Token
items.summary: Energy-efficient deployment of large language models requires understanding how model architecture, hardware, and serving settings shape energy per generated token. We introduce the Token-Energy Law, a compact, interpretable model of GPU-board energy per output token for dense, full-history decoding. It relates token energy to two core dimensions: active bytes and realized decode time. Active bytes describe logical byte demand per output, separating dense weights shared within a decode iteration from private key--value (KV) histories read and updated for each request. Realized decode time is the elapsed decode duration divided by the number of output tokens produced. We combine the two byte coordinates and time in a common affine form, with coefficients calibrated for each model and hardware/runtime configuration. This formulation explains how batching amortizes shared-weight work, longer attended histories increase private KV demand, and throughput determines the time-associated cost per output. Our experiments cover three models under BF16 decoding on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, including two-GPU tensor parallelism on Hopper. Using fixed coefficients and observed decode time, held-out condition-mean energy estimates differ from measurements by at most 3.73%.

items.title: Continuous-Time Policy Gradient from Discrete Data: Convergence Analysis and Model-Free Algorithms
items.summary: Continuous-time reinforcement learning seeks an optimal policy under unknown dynamics driven by stochastic differential equations using observations collected at discrete times. We develop a policy gradient framework that combines rigorous convergence analysis with learning from discrete data. We first establish a performance difference lemma and derive policy gradient formulas for randomized and parametrized policies. We then prove exponential convergence of an entropy-regularized policy flow to the regularized optimum. For discrete parametrized updates, we derive a convergence bound that explicitly separates the contributions of critic error, policy-regression error, and the learning step size. To enable learning under unknown dynamics, we integrate this framework with PhiBE, which constructs a continuous-time surrogate generator from discrete transition data. The resulting on-policy and off-policy model-free actor-critic algorithms preserve the continuous-time structure of the control problem. Numerical experiments on an entropy-regularized linear-quadratic regulator and a nonlinear wheeled robot demonstrate the performance and stability of the proposed methods with both known and data-driven dynamics.

items.title: PaPi: Parallel Picard-Duhamel Integration for Fast Neuro-Spectral Architectures
items.summary: Neuro-spectral architectures (NeuSA) are a class of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that have proven effective for solving time-dependent PDEs in the frequency domain. However, training and inference often rely on costly numerical integration of the learned vector field, typically using sequential Runge-Kutta time stepping, which limits temporal parallelism. We introduce PaPi, an integration scheme inspired by weakly nonlinear flows that enables time-Parallel inference through exponential integration and a Duhamel-Picard scheme. We show that the Duhamel-Picard iteration converges exponentially for all flows, and provide explicit error bounds that depend on how close the flow is to linear. Experiments show that PaPi accelerates training and inference by up to two orders of magnitude, achieving training times of under one second for low-dimensional PDE learning problems, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy.

items.title: Turning TS2Vec into a Foundation Model for Time Series Classification
items.summary: TS2Vec is one of the strongest self-supervised methods for time series classification, introduced in 2022. It is designed to be trained anew on every dataset: self-supervised pre-training followed by linear probing. Since then, the field has shifted towards foundation models that reuse one encoder across datasets. Yet TS2Vec offers a compact convolutional architecture that operates directly on temporal samples and accepts variable-length inputs without resampling. We ask whether these properties can be retained when the encoder is pre-trained only once, and show that they can: TS2Vec can essentially be turned into a foundation model. Three changes suffice: pre-train on a synthetic corpus, feed the encoder a raw amplitude view and an instance-normalized shape view of the input through two small stems, and distill one specialist encoder per view into a single encoder. The result, TS2Vec-FM, is a 1.6M-parameter dilated convolutional network that, kept frozen, reaches 83.3% on UCR-128 and 75.3% on UEA-27 under linear probing, within 0.3 pp of MantisV2, the current state of the art, and above TS2Vec trained separately on each target dataset. What we find most interesting is how different TS2Vec-FM is from other foundation models in design: near-parity is reached without attention, without a patch tokenizer, and without intermediate-layer extraction, using an "old-school" convolutional encoder and a two-layer MLP stem.

items.title: Efficient Edge-aware Attention Network for Graph Generation
items.summary: Graph generative models commonly use graph-specific Transformer architectures to jointly update node and edge features. However, these architectures do not directly benefit from recent hardware-aware attention implementations, limiting their scalability. The adaptation is, however, non-trivial: edge and graph-level features must be injected into pairwise attention scores, graph masks must be respected, and dynamic edge updates remain a major source of quadratic memory usage. We propose an edge-aware attention layer for graph generation that incorporates structural information through head-wise score modulation, while updating edge representations with a lightweight residual mechanism that retains attention-score dependent edge updates. This layer can be effectively implemented using PyTorch's FlexAttention. We achieve similar generation quality to our baseline while reducing peak GPU memory by around 65% and substantially improving training and sampling throughput. These results suggest that the proposed architecture is a practical step toward scalable graph foundation models.

items.title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
items.summary: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.

items.title: I Tested Four Local AI Models on a Literary Translation. Gemma 4 Won — With a Catch.
items.summary: I Tested Four Local AI Models on a Literary Translation. Gemma 4 Won — With a Catch. Four local GGUF models, one English novel, 20 matched passages — and a lesson in speed, Serbian grammar, and translation failure. I wanted to answer a practical question: if I have a Windows laptop with an NVIDIA GTX 1650 Ti and 4 GB of VRAM, which small local language model should I actually trust to translate an English novel into Serbian? The obvious candidate was TranslateGemma, a model designed for translation. But after its first run, I tried a general-purpose Gemma 4 model, followed by Qwen3 and Qwen3.5. I kept the source passages and translation instructions fixed, recorded each response and its timings, and inspected the Serbian that came back. The surprise was not only that Gemma 4 E2B finished fastest. It also completed every passage without a retry or script conversion. Yet when I read the translations, even the apparent winner produced invented words, awkward grammar, and meanings that drifted away from the English. A model can pass every automated check and still be a poor literary translator. The experiment: one old novel, four local models The source was The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom, an English-language literary work. The prepared TXT file contained 3,694 non-empty source lines representing 158,396 words. For this exploratory comparison, I sent exactly the first 20 non-empty lines to each model. Those lines contained 943 English words in total. “Line” matters here: these were not guaranteed to be individual grammatical sentences. Some contained several sentences, and some suffered from imperfect text preparation. For example, the source had joined boundaries such as “impracticable.Indeed” and “ostentation.I have”. These defects can make translation harder and limit what the results tell us. All four tests used Q4_K_M GGUF quantization on the same laptop and local llama.cpp server, with a configured context of 4,096 tokens. The request used temperature 0, seed 0, a 512-token output cap, sequential calls, and cache_prompt=false. Each model used its own available server-side chat formatting, so this was a comparison of practical local configurations — not a controlled isolation of neural-network weights. Models tested TranslateGemma 4B - translategemma-4b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf Gemma 4 E2B - google_gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf Qwen3 4B - Qwen3–4B-Q4_K_M.gguf Qwen3.5 4B - Qwen3.5–4B-Q4_K_M.gguf The English instruction asked for fluent Serbian in Latin script, preservation of literary style and meaning, and no commentary around the translation. I did not change its text between these four experiments: the recorded prompt SHA-256 matched across runs. First surprise: Gemma 4 E2B won the speed test For generation throughput, Gemma 4 E2B reached 59.65 output tokens per second. TranslateGemma reached 41.76, Qwen3 reached 40.06, and Qwen3.5 reached 34.62. In this setup, Gemma 4 generated approximately 43% more tokens per second than TranslateGemma and 72% more than Qwen3.5. Prompt processing showed the same general pattern: Gemma 4 E2B processed approximately 325.39 tokens/s; TranslateGemma, 209.74; Qwen3, 180.91; and Qwen3.5, 171.15. The elapsed runs tell an even clearer operational story. Gemma 4 took 38.95 seconds for the 20-passages test; TranslateGemma, 55.48 seconds; Qwen3.5, 117.16 seconds; and Qwen3, 147.59 seconds. These are wall-clock figures including failed requests and retry overhead — not just clean inference benchmarks. Mean latency for accepted translations was 1.81 seconds on Gemma 4, 2.63 seconds on TranslateGemma, 3.47 seconds on Qwen3.5, and 3.83 seconds on Qwen3. The respective 95th-percentile accepted-response latencies were 2.81, 4.06, 6.47, and 7.51 seconds. Those percentiles come from very small samples and should not be overinterpreted. There is a practical caveat: a 20-line batch cannot establish a universal performance ranking across all workloads. Also, the Qwen models produced unsuccessful responses and extra requests. Comparing elapsed total time is therefore a measure of end-to-end usefulness under this workflow, rather than architecture-only speed. Second surprise: a 100% pass rate does not mean good translation TranslateGemma accepted 20 of 20 lines. Gemma 4 also accepted 20 of 20. Qwen3.5 accepted 19 of 20, and Qwen3 accepted only 16 of 20. These were technical acceptance rates: the checks caught empty output, invalid scripts, truncation, some formatting leaks, and line-alignment problems. They did not judge whether the Serbian was elegant, grammatical, or faithful. That distinction became obvious as soon as I compared selected source passages with model outputs. The first passage: a clear win, followed by a warning The novel begins with a long sentence discussing how hard it is to write a dedication flattering a patron without inviting public ridicule. Near the end, the English says the task was “altogether impracticable”. TranslateGemma: "…bili saglasni da je ova zadata posta." Gemma 4: "…složili da je zadatak potpuno nemoguć." On that clause, Gemma 4 preserves the meaning; TranslateGemma does not. But the same Gemma 4 passage also contains “samopoželju patrona”, an unnatural and seemingly invented expression. A better local result is not automatically a publishable translation. A false friend in a literary context In another line, the source says: “In dedication, as in poetry, there is no medium…” Here “dedication” refers to the literary dedication; “no medium” means no middle ground. TranslateGemma returned “U čast, kao i u poeziji, nema sredstva…”. Gemma 4 returned “U posvećenju, kao i u poeziji, nema sredstva za to…”. Gemma 4 recognized the dedication context more closely, but both misread “no medium”. This is exactly the kind of error a generic script validator cannot catch: the output contains Serbian-looking words and still gets the passage wrong. When grammar changes the relationship between characters In a passage about the narrator’s affection and sincerity, TranslateGemma turned the intended relationship around with wording resembling “you are credible and sincere to me.” Gemma 4 came closer to the intended sense: the addressee is convinced of the narrator’s affection and sincerity. Yet its translation still used stiff constructions such as “ovaj adres”. Elsewhere, Gemma 4 produced “Osmešila sam se … i tremeo sam …”, switching grammatical gender and using a malformed verb in one sentence. On the phrase “disgrace and discomfiture of vice”, neither Gemma model expressed the moral meaning particularly well. The failures were not limited to spelling; they involved interpretation, register, and coherence. Serbian is not just Latin vs. Cyrillic Serbian can be written in Latin or Cyrillic script, and both Ekavian and Ijekavian are recognized pronunciation standards. My practical target, however, was consistent Serbian Latin in the Ekavian variety. That is a tighter constraint than simply producing something recognizable as Serbian. TranslateGemma’s accepted outputs included Ijekavian or regionally different forms such as “svijet”, “mjeri”, and “posljedice”. Gemma 4 generally leaned Ekavian in these examples but still made numerous grammatical mistakes; Qwen3.5 mixed forms such as “cijenimo” and “nedosljednost” with Ekavian forms elsewhere. To be precise, Ijekavian itself is not “incorrect Serbian”. The problem for this use case was inconsistency, sometimes combined with vocabulary drifting toward other closely related standards. A good editorial workflow would choose the desired variety up front, test for consistency, and still use human review. Mechanical spelling normalization cannot repair misunderstood sentences. The Cyrillic problem was real — and mostly fixable The first TranslateGemma prototype rejected every response containing Cyrillic. With temperature 0 and seed 0, retrying the same request three times tended to produce the same Cyrillic again. That wasted inference time without improving the answer. I changed the pipeline to retain each raw response and, when safe, transliterate Serbian Cyrillic into Latin as a separate postprocessing step. The transformation handles Serbian-specific letters and digraphs, including љ→lj, њ→nj, џ→dž, ђ→đ, ћ→ć, ч→č, ш→š, and ж→ž. The original model output stays in the attempt log, so native script behavior remains measurable. In the 20-line TranslateGemma test, five outputs needed transliteration (25%). All 20 were accepted without extra inference. Gemma 4 required none. Qwen3.5 also required none. Qwen3 accepted seven transliterated passages but generated some Cyrillic containing unsupported non-Serbian characters; three lines failed the script check despite repeated attempts. This improvement is useful, but not a linguistic quality fix. Transliteration changes the writing system, not the meaning. An incoherent sentence remains incoherent when rendered in Latin letters. The Qwen3.5 “nothing” loop: segment 4 The most memorable failure was passage four in the Qwen3.5 run. The source discusses an author who expresses genuine gratitude, only for the public to dismiss that praise as self-interest or flattery. Instead of finishing the translation, the model began repeating the Serbian word “ništa” (“nothing”) over and over. A short excerpt from the failed continuation: "…ništa ništa ništa ništa ništa ništa…" The three Qwen3.5 attempts each hit exactly 512 output tokens and ended with finish_reason=length. They repeated essentially the same degeneration because the prompt, seed, and decoding settings were unchanged. This was not evidence that the passage needed 512 useful tokens of translation; it was a generation loop. Increasing the cap to 1,024 would not address the underlying repetition by itself. The earlier Qwen3 run showed a similar pattern on passage five: three truncated responses at the token limit, alongside three separate lines failing script validation. Qwen3 thus ended with 16 accepted passages after 28 HTTP calls. Qwen3.5 finished with 19 accepted passages after 22 calls. An important engineering lesson followed: a retry policy should understand the error. Transport failures may deserve retries. Deterministic script violations and repetition loops need different treatment — perhaps model-specific decoding changes, bounded repetition detection, or explicit human review — not two automatic copies of the same failed request. What the numbers really say Under these exact local settings, Gemma 4 E2B was the strongest overall practical performer. It had the highest observed generation and prompt-processing throughput, the shortest end-to-end run, all 20 responses accepted, and no transliteration or retry overhead. On several passages, it also preserved the English meaning better than TranslateGemma. But it did not win literary translation in the stronger editorial sense. It still created strange words, mishandled idioms, lost grammatical agreement, and rendered nuanced prose awkwardly. TranslateGemma — the model with translation in its name — did not escape these problems either. Qwen3.5 delivered 19 technically acceptable lines, but quality defects and a repetition loop weakened its showing. Qwen3 was the least reliable configuration in this initial batch. None of this proves that one entire model family is “better” at Serbian, or that a different prompt, tokenizer configuration, decoding setup, or cleaned dataset would not change the ranking. The source sample was small, contiguous, and literary; it had text-preparation artifacts; and the models used different native chat templates. There was no independently curated Serbian reference translation, no BLEU/chrF++/COMET evaluation, and no blind multi-rater human scoring. These results are an honest pilot, not a publication-grade multilingual benchmark. items.summary_html:
I Tested Four Local AI Models on a Literary Translation. Gemma 4 Won — With a Catch.Four local GGUF models, one English novel, 20 matched passages — and a lesson in speed, Serbian grammar, and translation failure.

I wanted to answer a practical question: if I have a Windows laptop with an NVIDIA GTX 1650 Ti and 4 GB of VRAM, which small local language model should I actually trust to translate an English novel into Serbian?

The obvious candidate was TranslateGemma, a model designed for translation. But after its first run, I tried a general-purpose Gemma 4 model, followed by Qwen3 and Qwen3.5. I kept the source passages and translation instructions fixed, recorded each response and its timings, and inspected the Serbian that came back.

The surprise was not only that Gemma 4 E2B finished fastest. It also completed every passage without a retry or script conversion. Yet when I read the translations, even the apparent winner produced invented words, awkward grammar, and meanings that drifted away from the English. A model can pass every automated check and still be a poor literary translator.

The experiment: one old novel, four local models

The source was The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom, an English-language literary work. The prepared TXT file contained 3,694 non-empty source lines representing 158,396 words. For this exploratory comparison, I sent exactly the first 20 non-empty lines to each model. Those lines contained 943 English words in total.

“Line” matters here: these were not guaranteed to be individual grammatical sentences. Some contained several sentences, and some suffered from imperfect text preparation. For example, the source had joined boundaries such as “impracticable.Indeed” and “ostentation.I have”. These defects can make translation harder and limit what the results tell us.

All four tests used Q4_K_M GGUF quantization on the same laptop and local llama.cpp server, with a configured context of 4,096 tokens. The request used temperature 0, seed 0, a 512-token output cap, sequential calls, and cache_prompt=false. Each model used its own available server-side chat formatting, so this was a comparison of practical local configurations — not a controlled isolation of neural-network weights.

Models tested

TranslateGemma 4B - translategemma-4b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf
Gemma 4 E2B - google_gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf
Qwen3 4B - Qwen3–4B-Q4_K_M.gguf
Qwen3.5 4B - Qwen3.5–4B-Q4_K_M.gguf

The English instruction asked for fluent Serbian in Latin script, preservation of literary style and meaning, and no commentary around the translation. I did not change its text between these four experiments: the recorded prompt SHA-256 matched across runs.

First surprise: Gemma 4 E2B won the speed test

For generation throughput, Gemma 4 E2B reached 59.65 output tokens per second. TranslateGemma reached 41.76, Qwen3 reached 40.06, and Qwen3.5 reached 34.62. In this setup, Gemma 4 generated approximately 43% more tokens per second than TranslateGemma and 72% more than Qwen3.5.

Prompt processing showed the same general pattern: Gemma 4 E2B processed approximately 325.39 tokens/s; TranslateGemma, 209.74; Qwen3, 180.91; and Qwen3.5, 171.15.

The elapsed runs tell an even clearer operational story. Gemma 4 took 38.95 seconds for the 20-passages test; TranslateGemma, 55.48 seconds; Qwen3.5, 117.16 seconds; and Qwen3, 147.59 seconds. These are wall-clock figures including failed requests and retry overhead — not just clean inference benchmarks.

Mean latency for accepted translations was 1.81 seconds on Gemma 4, 2.63 seconds on TranslateGemma, 3.47 seconds on Qwen3.5, and 3.83 seconds on Qwen3. The respective 95th-percentile accepted-response latencies were 2.81, 4.06, 6.47, and 7.51 seconds. Those percentiles come from very small samples and should not be overinterpreted.

There is a practical caveat: a 20-line batch cannot establish a universal performance ranking across all workloads. Also, the Qwen models produced unsuccessful responses and extra requests. Comparing elapsed total time is therefore a measure of end-to-end usefulness under this workflow, rather than architecture-only speed.

Second surprise: a 100% pass rate does not mean good translation

TranslateGemma accepted 20 of 20 lines. Gemma 4 also accepted 20 of 20. Qwen3.5 accepted 19 of 20, and Qwen3 accepted only 16 of 20. These were technical acceptance rates: the checks caught empty output, invalid scripts, truncation, some formatting leaks, and line-alignment problems. They did not judge whether the Serbian was elegant, grammatical, or faithful.

That distinction became obvious as soon as I compared selected source passages with model outputs.

The first passage: a clear win, followed by a warning

The novel begins with a long sentence discussing how hard it is to write a dedication flattering a patron without inviting public ridicule. Near the end, the English says the task was “altogether impracticable”.

TranslateGemma: "…bili saglasni da je ova zadata posta."
Gemma 4: "…složili da je zadatak potpuno nemoguć."

On that clause, Gemma 4 preserves the meaning; TranslateGemma does not. But the same Gemma 4 passage also contains “samopoželju patrona”, an unnatural and seemingly invented expression. A better local result is not automatically a publishable translation.

A false friend in a literary context

In another line, the source says: “In dedication, as in poetry, there is no medium…” Here “dedication” refers to the literary dedication; “no medium” means no middle ground. TranslateGemma returned “U čast, kao i u poeziji, nema sredstva…”. Gemma 4 returned “U posvećenju, kao i u poeziji, nema sredstva za to…”.

Gemma 4 recognized the dedication context more closely, but both misread “no medium”. This is exactly the kind of error a generic script validator cannot catch: the output contains Serbian-looking words and still gets the passage wrong.

When grammar changes the relationship between characters

In a passage about the narrator’s affection and sincerity, TranslateGemma turned the intended relationship around with wording resembling “you are credible and sincere to me.” Gemma 4 came closer to the intended sense: the addressee is convinced of the narrator’s affection and sincerity. Yet its translation still used stiff constructions such as “ovaj adres”.

Elsewhere, Gemma 4 produced “Osmešila sam se … i tremeo sam …”, switching grammatical gender and using a malformed verb in one sentence. On the phrase “disgrace and discomfiture of vice”, neither Gemma model expressed the moral meaning particularly well. The failures were not limited to spelling; they involved interpretation, register, and coherence.

Serbian is not just Latin vs. Cyrillic

Serbian can be written in Latin or Cyrillic script, and both Ekavian and Ijekavian are recognized pronunciation standards. My practical target, however, was consistent Serbian Latin in the Ekavian variety. That is a tighter constraint than simply producing something recognizable as Serbian.

TranslateGemma’s accepted outputs included Ijekavian or regionally different forms such as “svijet”, “mjeri”, and “posljedice”. Gemma 4 generally leaned Ekavian in these examples but still made numerous grammatical mistakes; Qwen3.5 mixed forms such as “cijenimo” and “nedosljednost” with Ekavian forms elsewhere.

To be precise, Ijekavian itself is not “incorrect Serbian”. The problem for this use case was inconsistency, sometimes combined with vocabulary drifting toward other closely related standards. A good editorial workflow would choose the desired variety up front, test for consistency, and still use human review. Mechanical spelling normalization cannot repair misunderstood sentences.

The Cyrillic problem was real — and mostly fixable

The first TranslateGemma prototype rejected every response containing Cyrillic. With temperature 0 and seed 0, retrying the same request three times tended to produce the same Cyrillic again. That wasted inference time without improving the answer.

I changed the pipeline to retain each raw response and, when safe, transliterate Serbian Cyrillic into Latin as a separate postprocessing step. The transformation handles Serbian-specific letters and digraphs, including љ→lj, њ→nj, џ→dž, ђ→đ, ћ→ć, ч→č, ш→š, and ж→ž. The original model output stays in the attempt log, so native script behavior remains measurable.

In the 20-line TranslateGemma test, five outputs needed transliteration (25%). All 20 were accepted without extra inference. Gemma 4 required none. Qwen3.5 also required none. Qwen3 accepted seven transliterated passages but generated some Cyrillic containing unsupported non-Serbian characters; three lines failed the script check despite repeated attempts.

This improvement is useful, but not a linguistic quality fix. Transliteration changes the writing system, not the meaning. An incoherent sentence remains incoherent when rendered in Latin letters.

The Qwen3.5 “nothing” loop: segment 4

The most memorable failure was passage four in the Qwen3.5 run. The source discusses an author who expresses genuine gratitude, only for the public to dismiss that praise as self-interest or flattery. Instead of finishing the translation, the model began repeating the Serbian word “ništa” (“nothing”) over and over.

A short excerpt from the failed continuation: "…ništa ništa ništa ništa ništa ništa…"

The three Qwen3.5 attempts each hit exactly 512 output tokens and ended with finish_reason=length. They repeated essentially the same degeneration because the prompt, seed, and decoding settings were unchanged. This was not evidence that the passage needed 512 useful tokens of translation; it was a generation loop. Increasing the cap to 1,024 would not address the underlying repetition by itself.

The earlier Qwen3 run showed a similar pattern on passage five: three truncated responses at the token limit, alongside three separate lines failing script validation. Qwen3 thus ended with 16 accepted passages after 28 HTTP calls. Qwen3.5 finished with 19 accepted passages after 22 calls.

An important engineering lesson followed: a retry policy should understand the error. Transport failures may deserve retries. Deterministic script violations and repetition loops need different treatment — perhaps model-specific decoding changes, bounded repetition detection, or explicit human review — not two automatic copies of the same failed request.

What the numbers really say

Under these exact local settings, Gemma 4 E2B was the strongest overall practical performer. It had the highest observed generation and prompt-processing throughput, the shortest end-to-end run, all 20 responses accepted, and no transliteration or retry overhead. On several passages, it also preserved the English meaning better than TranslateGemma.

But it did not win literary translation in the stronger editorial sense. It still created strange words, mishandled idioms, lost grammatical agreement, and rendered nuanced prose awkwardly. TranslateGemma — the model with translation in its name — did not escape these problems either. Qwen3.5 delivered 19 technically acceptable lines, but quality defects and a repetition loop weakened its showing. Qwen3 was the least reliable configuration in this initial batch.

None of this proves that one entire model family is “better” at Serbian, or that a different prompt, tokenizer configuration, decoding setup, or cleaned dataset would not change the ranking. The source sample was small, contiguous, and literary; it had text-preparation artifacts; and the models used different native chat templates. There was no independently curated Serbian reference translation, no BLEU/chrF++/COMET evaluation, and no blind multi-rater human scoring. These results are an honest pilot, not a publication-grade multilingual benchmark.

What I would change in a production translation pipeline

Clean the source text first, restoring lost spaces and separating real sentences before testing sentence-level batching.

Keep raw model responses, normalized outputs, prompt hashes, token timing, and exact model/server metadata for every request.

Treat script compliance, language-variety consistency, and semantic fidelity as three different checks.

Use targeted handling for repeated tokens and output truncation; stop repeating deterministic failures automatically.

Ask bilingual reviewers to score meaning, grammar, terminology, and style on a larger, stratified sample before translating an entire book.

The infrastructure already stores aligned source/target lines, checkpoint state, per-attempt CSV data, and machine-readable summaries. That made the failures as informative as the successes. Without those records, I would have had four vague impressions about models. With them, I could show exactly where and how each system broke.

My takeaway

The fastest model was also the most usable one in this small test: Gemma 4 E2B. But that is only half the story. Translation success is not the same as generating Latin-script Serbian text at 60 tokens per second. The real test is whether a native reader can trust the meaning, register, grammar, and voice.

If I were building a local, private, low-cost translation assistant on this laptop today, Gemma 4 would be my first candidate for a human-in-the-loop workflow — not for unattended publication of a classic novel. The biggest improvement might not come from another few tokens per second. It might come from better source preparation, better error handling, and a serious evaluation of the words the models actually write.

Experiment notes and sources

Hardware: NVIDIA GTX 1650 Ti Laptop GPU (4 GB VRAM), Windows, local llama.cpp server. Model files were quantized GGUF Q4_K_M. Sample: first 20 non-empty lines of The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom (943 source words). Recorded llama.cpp build: b8729–243532e55. Settings: context 4096, max_tokens 512, temperature 0, seed 0, sequential requests, cache_prompt=false. Chat templates differed by model; all four runs share the same prompt SHA-256.

Metrics are taken from four local checkpointed experiment reports and their per-attempt records, dated October 20, 2026. Aggregate output-token rates are computed from paired server token counts and generation times for successful first attempts. Wall-clock duration includes failed/retried work. No quality metric was calculated from a reference corpus.

Further Reading

If you’re interested in exploring local language models, machine translation, and the challenges of evaluating multilingual AI systems, these resources provide useful technical background.

  1. TranslateGemma: A New Suite of Open Translation Models — Google
    Google’s introduction to TranslateGemma, a family of specialized translation models designed for multilingual communication across 55 languages. Useful for understanding the motivation behind the translation-focused model included in this experiment.
  2. Gemma 4 Model Card — Google DeepMind
    Official technical documentation covering Gemma 4’s architecture, multilingual capabilities, model sizes, and intended applications. Provides background on the Gemma 4 E2B model that achieved the strongest overall practical results in our small-scale test.
  3. Qwen3.5–4B — Official Model Documentation
    The official model documentation, including inference configuration and thinking versus non-thinking modes. Particularly relevant to investigating generation behavior, response truncation, and repetition loops.
  4. FLORES-200: A Multilingual Machine Translation Benchmark — Meta AI Research
    A multilingual evaluation benchmark designed to measure translation performance across a wide range of languages. It provides a useful starting point for building more systematic translation-quality experiments beyond a small collection of literary passages.
  5. Scaling Neural Machine Translation to 200 Languages — Nature
    A research paper on multilingual machine translation at scale. Its discussion of evaluation methodology and metrics such as chrF++ is particularly relevant to distinguishing measurable translation accuracy from grammatical fluency and literary quality.

These resources provide the broader context for a central finding of this experiment: fast inference, technically valid output, and high-quality literary translation are three different things.

items.title: I Built a Local AI Chrome Extension. The Llama API Was the Easy Part.
items.summary: How a prompt-improvement button taught me about Chrome extensions, ProseMirror, local Llama APIs, and the challenges of reliable AI tools. I started with an idea that sounded almost trivial: add an “Improve Prompt” button to ChatGPT, send the draft to a local language model, and let the user replace the original with a clearer version. No cloud API subscription. No complicated application framework. Just a Chrome extension and a local llama.cpp server. The model integration worked surprisingly quickly. The difficult part was everything around it: identifying the real editor, preserving structured text, keeping the interface from breaking, preventing late responses from overwriting newer drafts, and deciding what “tested” actually means when software interacts with a changing website. This is the engineering story of Local Prompt Enhancer: what I built, what broke during review, what the tests caught, and what remains to be validated before a public release. The initial idea: improve the draft, not the conversation The intended workflow was deliberately small: write a prompt, click Improve Prompt, send that text to a locally running model, review the suggestion, and choose whether to apply it. The extension never needs to send the message to ChatGPT on the user’s behalf. That last detail matters. A prompt editor should not become an invisible intermediary with permission to submit conversations. A suggestion panel with Apply, Copy, and Cancel keeps a person in control of the final request. I used a llama.cpp server listening on 127.0.0.1:8080 and tested the API adapter against a local Gemma GGUF model, google_gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf. The extension calls the OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint; it is separate from the ChatGPT API. Lesson 1: the visible input box is not the real input box My first instinct was to look for a CSS class associated with ChatGPT’s composer. In the inspected page, one wrapper was named ComposerLayoutBody-uBBf1A. That looked promising, but it was only the surrounding layout. The editable element was a ProseMirror-backed contenteditable node, identified more reliably through attributes such as role=”textbox” and data-composer-markdown. Generated class names can change after a frontend update, so treating them as stable extension APIs is a maintenance trap. const editor = document.querySelector( '[data-composer-input] [contenteditable="true"][role="textbox"]' ); The practical lesson: use a selector strategy with fallbacks, check that the editor is connected and visible, and be prepared for it to be replaced during navigation. A MutationObserver can help reattach controls, but it must not create duplicate buttons or expensive mutation loops. I also learned that reading rich text is not the same as reading a textarea’s value. Paragraph breaks, nested lists, fenced code, URLs, Windows paths, and intentional blank lines all require care. A prompt enhancer that silently corrupts code or paths has failed before the language model even runs. Lesson 2: Manifest V3 is a separation-of-responsibilities exercise The first working architecture used plain JavaScript and Chrome Manifest V3. I intentionally avoided React, Vite, and npm packages for the MVP. That kept installation simple: Chrome could load the project directly as an unpacked extension. The content script handles ChatGPT’s editor and the Shadow DOM interface. The background service worker validates messages and makes the local HTTP request. A separate API module handles model discovery, timeout, response parsing, and error reporting. Settings live in chrome.storage.local. Content script → MV3 service worker → 127.0.0.1:8080 ← improved prompt ← llama.cpp The boundary is useful for both security and maintenance. The content script does not need to fetch the model endpoint directly, and the worker does not need to manipulate ChatGPT’s DOM. Host permissions can remain limited to the local server instead of requesting access to arbitrary websites. That approach also made the code easier to test. I could mock the HTTP adapter independently of the editor, and I could test messaging without running an actual language model every time. Lesson 3: stateless prompting makes the behavior explainable For the first version, every Llama call included a complete editing instruction and the user’s current draft. No earlier conversation was supplied. The model was told to correct grammar, improve clarity and structure, preserve original meaning and technical details, and return only the rewritten prompt — not an answer to the prompt itself. messages: [ { role: "system", content: COMPLETE_EDITING_INSTRUCTION }, { role: "user", content: capturedDraft } ] This is more than a prompt-engineering preference. It makes each request reproducible and reduces accidental context leakage. The model cannot rely on instructions that happened to be sent in a previous call. The API client also discovers the loaded model through /v1/models rather than assuming that a local GGUF filename is universally valid. It rejects malformed responses and truncated generations and surfaces failures in the interface rather than replacing the draft with unreliable output. One subtle bug appeared in review: trimming the returned text removed leading indentation and trailing blank lines. For prose, that may seem harmless. For a prompt that contains code, it is a correctness defect. The hardened implementation preserves the meaningful whitespace and normalizes line endings. Lesson 4: Apply is more dangerous than Improve Generating a suggestion is easy to reverse: if the user dislikes it, they can simply ignore the preview. Replacing text inside a rich editor is different. The website maintains its own editor state and undo history; writing directly to innerHTML or textContent can make the visible DOM disagree with that state. The MVP uses a native editing operation, document.execCommand(“insertText”), rather than replacing the editor’s HTML. That command is deprecated, so it is a compatibility choice, not a future-proof integration API. The hardened Apply path checks that the same editor is still present, that the draft has not changed, and that the editor can actually receive focus. It then attempts the edit and verifies the resulting text. If replacement cannot be trusted, the extension leaves a Copy fallback and an original-text recovery field. The remaining limitation is important: two checks of visible text do not prove that ProseMirror’s private state and undo stack are healthy. Only live-browser tests — Apply, keep typing, change focus, return to the draft, and use Ctrl+Z — can establish acceptable real-world behavior. This became my clearest design principle: a writing assistant must be conservative about editing someone else’s draft. Lesson 5: asynchronous requests need identities, not just loading spinners Local models can take time to respond. In that interval, users may type, navigate, cancel, open another chat, or try again. Without explicit request identities, a late result can appear in the wrong context or a cancelled request can leave the interface permanently busy. The first version already used an AbortController, loading state, and changed-draft protection. Review exposed a cancellation race: Cancel aborted the fetch, but the worker’s active-request slot remained occupied until asynchronous cleanup finished. A new request could receive BUSY even though the user had cancelled the old one. The fix was conceptually small: remove the active slot immediately on cancellation, abort the matching controller, and make completion cleanup conditional on request identity. That way, an old request cannot clear the slot belonging to a newer request. if (active.get(key)?.id === requestId) { const old = active.get(key); active.delete(key); old.controller.abort(); } An equally important rule is never to apply a suggestion if the draft changed during inference — even if the user later undid those edits and the visible text matches again. The interface records that the draft was touched, not merely whether its final string happens to match a snapshot. Service worker lifecycle rules add another constraint. Long model inference can outlive a browser extension worker’s reliable fetch window. The project therefore uses explicit timeout and channel-error handling, without silently retrying an inference request. That behavior still needs real Chrome validation with slow responses. Lesson 6: local AI is not the same as zero-risk AI Using a loopback endpoint is attractive because the extension does not need a third-party inference service. But “local” is a deployment property, not a magic privacy guarantee. A server accidentally bound to a public network interface, a permissive proxy, or verbose server logging can change the risk profile. The extension limits its configured API origin to http://127.0.0.1:8080, omits credentials from fetch calls, rejects redirects, validates message sources, and renders model output as text rather than executable HTML. It reads the draft when the user requests improvement rather than sending each keystroke for processing. Those decisions are valuable, but they do not eliminate the need for a truthful privacy policy before publication. Users should know that the product requires their own running local server and that its logging and network exposure remain under their control. Lesson 7: 45 passing tests are encouraging — not a browser certificate The first implementation was accompanied by 20 dependency-free tests. An API smoke test also returned a successful rewrite using the local Gemma model. After reviewing the code, I expanded the suite to 45 tests, adding 25 regression cases covering nested lists, whitespace, focus changes, cancellation races, stale results, composer recreation, shared limits, and timeout recovery. The tests mattered because they captured the defects that ordinary happy-path demos conceal. They also provided a clean way to verify small fixes without accidentally breaking the model adapter or request lifecycle. But those were mostly Node-based tests using controlled DOM and Chrome API doubles. A fake DOM cannot tell me whether the actual ChatGPT Send button is visually overlapped, whether native undo behaves correctly, or whether the real ProseMirror editor reconciles a replacement after several seconds. At the time of this write-up, live Chrome acceptance testing was still outstanding. Claiming the extension was production-ready because the automated suite passed would have confused test coverage with evidence of user-facing reliability. The proper acceptance sequence is straightforward: load the unpacked extension, verify model connectivity, generate a preview, Apply a single paragraph, test multiline code, continue typing, undo, cancel and restart, navigate between chats, and inspect both the ChatGPT console and the extension service worker. Lesson 8: “Retry” and “Refine Further” describe different products A basic Retry starts a new independent rewrite of the current draft. It may produce different wording because text generation is not necessarily deterministic, but it does not learn from its previous answer. Calling that refinement would be misleading. The next design iteration introduces a more deliberate Refine Further flow. The planned request includes only two text artifacts: the original user draft and the immediately preceding successful improvement. The editing instruction asks the model to improve the previous attempt while using the original as the source of truth. First pass: original → version 1 Refine further: original + version 1 → version 2 Refine again: original + version 2 → version 3 A small temperature increase, such as from 0.2 to 0.3, can permit different wording, but it cannot guarantee a better response. A good refinement instruction must allow the model to keep an already strong version mostly unchanged. Otherwise repeated refinement can drift away from what the user actually asked. This is a design direction described during the project, not a claim that every part of the new refinement flow has already passed end-to-end browser testing. Lesson 9: publishing is a different milestone from building Once the core extension was in place, the conversation shifted toward a Chrome Web Store release: recognizable PNG icons, a toolbar popup, a model connectivity indicator, onboarding, a privacy policy, store listing assets, and a clean ZIP package. These are not decorative extras. A product that depends on a separately running llama.cpp server needs to explain that dependency before users install it. A toolbar status display can make a disconnected server understandable rather than mysterious. A narrowly scoped permissions list and accurate store description build trust. The release preparation work was planned around a lightweight v0.2.0 candidate, while retaining the dependency-free extension architecture. Preparing a submission package is not the same thing as a confirmed Chrome Web Store publication or approval. What I would do differently next time · Design the “never automatically submit” rule before writing any UI code. It simplifies the entire trust model. · Write down the editor’s real DOM structure early, but treat selectors as hypotheses that need ongoing browser checks. · Make text preservation a first-class test requirement, especially for code, paths, lists, and blank lines. · Use unique IDs for every asynchronous request from the beginning; cancellation and navigation become much easier to reason about. · Separate API success, mocked browser behavior, and actual browser acceptance in every test report. · Keep a Copy fallback whenever integration with a third-party rich-text editor is uncertain. · Do not add frameworks before the interface actually needs them. Plain JavaScript was sufficient for this stage. The bigger takeaway This project began as a tiny local-AI feature and became a useful example of a broader engineering truth: the model call is often the least complicated part of an AI product. The real work is defining boundaries. Which element owns the user’s text? When is it safe to replace that text? What happens if the page changes while inference is running? How do you preserve intent and formatting? What counts as evidence that the software works? For Local Prompt Enhancer, the answer is not a larger model or a more elaborate frontend. It is a restrained workflow, explicit state management, testable modules, and a clear distinction between what has been implemented and what has been validated. That is the lesson I will carry into the next iteration — and into other applications that connect local AI models to existing software.
